title: Hiragana: the base syllabary
explanation: Hiragana is the set of 46 core rounded characters (plus dakuten/handakuten marks and small-kana combinations) that spells every native Japanese word and grammatical ending. It's the first script to learn because it encodes the mora — the basic timing unit Japanese conjugation is built on.

examples.native: あ、い、う、え、お
examples.gloss: a, i, u, e, o — the five base vowels hiragana is built from.

examples.native: たべます
examples.gloss: (I) eat. — a whole verb form written entirely in hiragana.

bridge_note: English spells sounds with an alphabet of individual consonants and vowels that combine in irregular ways. Hiragana instead gives each consonant+vowel pairing (or bare vowel) its own single symbol, so spelling is almost perfectly phonetic once you know the 46 shapes.
mistake: Treating hiragana as optional once kanji is learned — grammatical endings, particles, and many native words are written in hiragana permanently, never replaced by kanji.
source: Genki I Lesson 1 (kana charts); JF Standard N5 can-do

title: Katakana: the script for loanwords and emphasis
explanation: Katakana covers the exact same sounds as hiragana but with angular, distinct shapes, and is reserved for loanwords, onomatopoeia, and emphasis (similar to how English uses italics). Recognizing it lets a learner instantly spot borrowed vocabulary in a sentence.

examples.native: コーヒーを飲みます。
examples.gloss: I drink coffee.

examples.native: テレビを見ます。
examples.gloss: I watch TV.

bridge_note: English has no script-level way to flag "this word is foreign" — a loanword like "karaoke" just looks like any other English word. Japanese marks that status visually by switching scripts entirely.
mistake: Writing loanwords in hiragana instead of katakana, or vice versa — native Japanese words in katakana read as unusually emphatic or shouted.
source: Genki I Lesson 1 (kana charts); JF Standard N5 can-do

title: Kanji: logographic characters with two reading types
explanation: Kanji are characters borrowed from Chinese that represent whole words or word-roots rather than sounds. Most kanji have at least one on'yomi (a Chinese-derived reading, used in compounds) and one kun'yomi (a native Japanese reading, often used alone or with hiragana endings); N5 requires roughly 100 kanji.

examples.native: 山 (やま, san/zan)
examples.gloss: mountain — kun'yomi "yama" alone, on'yomi "san" in compounds like 富士山 (Mt. Fuji).

examples.native: 日本語を勉強します。
examples.gloss: I study Japanese.

bridge_note: English spells one word one way, full stop. A single kanji can be pronounced several different ways depending on context and neighboring characters — closer to how a Roman numeral or an ampersand carries a fixed meaning but can be read differently aloud.
mistake: Assuming a kanji has one fixed pronunciation and trying to sound out unfamiliar compounds letter-by-letter instead of learning each reading as its own vocabulary item.
source: Genki I/II kanji lists; JF Standard N5 can-do (~100 kanji)

title: Mora timing and special morae (long vowels, っ, ん)
explanation: Japanese rhythm is counted in morae — short, evenly-timed beats — rather than in syllables, so a long vowel, a small っ (geminate consonant), or the moraic ん each add one full extra beat instead of just coloring the syllable before them. Missing this timing changes word meaning, not just accent.

examples.native: おばさん / おばあさん
examples.gloss: aunt / grandmother — distinguished only by one extra vowel-length beat.

examples.native: きって
examples.gloss: stamp — the small っ holds the "t" sound for one extra beat before releasing it.

bridge_note: English is stress-timed, so speakers naturally compress or swallow unstressed vowels. Japanese gives every mora equal weight, so "shujin" (husband) and "shūjin" (prisoner) are genuinely different words, not the same word said slightly differently.
mistake: Collapsing long and short vowels because English stress-timing makes unstressed vowels feel disposable — producing 主人 (husband) when 囚人 (prisoner) was intended, or vice versa.
source: Genki I Lesson 1 pronunciation notes; JF Standard N5 can-do

title: Pitch accent awareness
explanation: Japanese distinguishes some words purely by which mora carries a pitch drop, not by stress or vowel quality — a system totally different from English intonation. At the beginner stage the goal is simply to notice this exists, not to master every word's pattern.

examples.native: 箸 (はし, high-low)
examples.gloss: chopsticks — pitch drops after the first mora.

examples.native: 橋 (はし, low-high)
examples.gloss: bridge — identical spelling and vowels to "chopsticks," distinguished only by pitch (rises instead of falling).

bridge_note: English uses stress (louder, longer syllables) to distinguish words like "CONtent" (noun) vs. "conTENT" (adjective) or to convey emotion. Japanese pitch accent is a separate, quieter system — a rise or fall in musical pitch on specific morae — that can change a word's meaning entirely while the loudness stays flat.
mistake: Applying English stress patterns (loudness on one syllable) instead of a pitch-level change, which makes Japanese sound accented even when every mora and consonant is otherwise correct.
source: General phonology of Japanese; not a specific JLPT-tested item at N5
long_form:
English speakers reflexively think of "accent" as loudness — the syllable you hit harder and hold longer, the way "CONtent" (the noun, satisfaction) and "conTENT" (the adjective, what's inside a box) are distinguished purely by which syllable gets stressed. Japanese pitch accent is a completely different mechanism operating on a completely different acoustic dimension: instead of loudness, it's the shape of pitch — where in the word the voice's musical pitch rises or falls — and, crucially, loudness stays essentially flat across the whole word regardless of which mora carries the accent. 箸 (hashi, chopsticks) and 橋 (hashi, bridge) are spelled identically in romaji, contain the exact same two morae, and are pronounced with identical vowel quality and equal loudness on both syllables — the only thing separating them is whether the pitch starts high and drops after the first mora, or starts low and rises into the second. This is why native English speakers who nail every consonant and vowel in a Japanese sentence can still sound unmistakably foreign: they're unconsciously layering English-style stress (loudness peaks) onto words that need pitch movement instead, and the two systems don't overlap enough to fake one with the other.

Pitch accent is often introduced to learners as a source of "chopsticks versus bridge"-style minimal pairs, which makes it sound like an occasional party trick rather than a structural feature — but it is worth knowing that pitch accent operates on every single word in the standard Tokyo dialect, all the time, whether or not that particular word happens to have a homophone it needs distinguishing from. Every word has a lexically specified accent pattern (Tokyo Japanese linguists classify words by which mora, if any, carries the pitch drop — some words have no drop at all, called heiban or "flat" pattern), and that pattern is just as much a fixed, memorizable property of the word as its vowels are. It's genuinely a separate layer of the phonology sitting on top of the mora-timing system from Unit 1, not a decoration on it — which is also exactly why the curriculum places pitch-accent awareness immediately after mora timing rather than as a much later refinement: both systems operate on the mora as their basic unit, and a learner who hasn't internalized what a mora is has no stable unit to hang a pitch pattern onto in the first place.

It's also worth being honest that pitch accent varies significantly by dialect — the patterns described here, and cited in most textbooks, are specifically standard (Tokyo-based) Japanese; Kansai dialect and others assign pitch quite differently to the same words, which is one visible, audible fingerprint of regional identity in spoken Japanese the way regional vowel shifts function in English. This is part of why the curriculum deliberately sets the bar at "awareness, not mastery" for beginners: getting every word's pitch pattern letter-perfect is a years-long project even for advanced learners, dictionaries that mark pitch accent are a specialist tool most textbooks skip entirely, and the practical payoff of imperfect pitch accent is usually just a foreign-sounding but perfectly intelligible accent, not actual miscommunication — real ambiguity from a pitch-accent minimal pair almost always gets resolved by context in a full sentence. The realistic goal at this stage is narrower and more achievable: training your ear to notice that Japanese pitch does something at all, so that later, more serious pitch-accent study has something to attach to instead of starting from the assumption that Japanese "doesn't really have accent" the way careless treatments sometimes imply.

The common mistake flagged in the short explanation — importing English stress patterns wholesale — deserves one more layer of nuance: it's not simply that learners put stress in the wrong place, it's that they impose a phenomenon (loudness-based stress) that the target language's phonology doesn't use for lexical contrast at all, the way a fluent French speaker mapping English's word stress onto French (which uses phrase-final stress instead of lexical stress) produces a specific, recognizable "foreign" quality distinct from simply mispronouncing sounds. Once you can hear Japanese pitch as pitch — a genuinely tonal-adjacent property, more like the rise and fall of a question in English than like syllable stress — the whole system stops sounding mysterious and starts sounding like exactly what it is: a small, closed, learnable set of pitch shapes layered onto a mora-timed language, doing a job English handles with an entirely different toolkit.

title: Rendaku: sequential voicing in compounds
explanation: When two native Japanese words combine into a compound, the first consonant of the second word often "voices" (k→g, t→d, s→z, h→b): 折り (ori, "fold") + 紙 (kami, "paper") becomes 折り紙 (origami). This same voicing shows up later in counter-number combinations.

examples.native: 折り紙 (おりがみ)
examples.gloss: origami — ori + kami, with kami voicing to gami.

examples.native: 人々 (ひとびと)
examples.gloss: people (plural) — hito + hito, with the second hito voicing to bito.

bridge_note: English compounds ("toothbrush," "bookshelf") never change the sound of the second word when it's glued to the first. Japanese does, and historically this voicing was the very signal that told listeners "this is one fused word," not two words said side by side.
mistake: Not recognizing a rendaku-voiced word as related to its plain form in the dictionary — looking up がみ instead of かみ and finding nothing.
source: General historical phonology of Japanese compounds
long_form:
Rendaku looks, at first glance, like an arbitrary spelling irregularity you just have to memorize word by word — origami instead of "orikami," hitobito instead of "hitohito" — but it is actually one of the more well-understood pieces of historical Japanese phonology, and knowing the mechanism turns a pile of memorized exceptions into a predictable (if not perfectly exceptionless) pattern. The rule: when two native Japanese morphemes fuse into a single compound word, the initial consonant of the second element voices — k becomes g, t becomes d, s becomes z, h becomes b — provided nothing blocks it. 折り (ori, "fold") + 紙 (kami, "paper") voices to 折り紙 (origami); 人 (hito) doubled as 人々 (hitobito) voices the second occurrence.

The historical explanation is genuinely satisfying and worth knowing even though a beginner doesn't need it to use the rule correctly: native Japanese vocabulary (the yamato-kotoba layer, as opposed to kanji compounds borrowed wholesale from Chinese) simply never began a word with a voiced obstruent — there was no native word that started with g, z, d, or b. That gap in the phoneme inventory meant that voicing the first consonant of a word was, for centuries, an unambiguous signal that this could not be a standalone word — it had to be the second half of a compound, fused onto something before it. Rendaku's voicing wasn't originally a rule speakers applied on purpose; it was a natural byproduct of two morphemes running together in fluent speech (a very ordinary kind of sound change called intervocalic voicing, familiar from many languages), and it survived as a marker specifically because the resulting voiced-initial shape was otherwise meaningless in isolation — there was no competing plain word it could be confused with.

Modern Japanese vocabulary has since imported plenty of loanwords and Chinese-derived readings that do begin with voiced consonants, so the original disambiguating function of rendaku has weakened, and the rule itself has picked up known exceptions and blocking conditions over the centuries. The best-known blocker is Lyman's Law: rendaku is suppressed if the second element already contains a voiced obstruent later in the word, which is why 山 (yama) + 風 (kaze, "wind") does not rendaku-voice into 山がぜ — かぜ already has a voiced consonant, so the whole compound resists the change. There are also plenty of compounds that simply resist rendaku for lexicalized, unpredictable reasons, and Sino-Japanese (on'yomi) compounds follow their own partially overlapping but distinct set of tendencies. None of this needs to be memorized at the beginner level — the point of introducing rendaku early is narrower and more practical: recognizing that がみ in a compound is really かみ in disguise, so that a learner encountering an unfamiliar word doesn't waste time looking up a nonexistent dictionary entry for がみ when the entry they need is under か.

The reason the curriculum resurfaces rendaku specifically at the counters unit (numbers combining with classifiers: 一本 ippon, 三本 sanbon, 六本 roppon) is that Japanese numeral-counter combinations are one of the last places in the modern language where the old sound-change machinery — rendaku plus its cousin, consonant gemination (the small っ that doubles a following consonant) — is still fully productive and grammatically obligatory rather than a fossilized lexical quirk. Once a learner has the historical picture — voicing marks compound-internal fusion, gemination smooths certain consonant clusters, and both concentrate around the same handful of numbers (1, 3, 6, 8, 10) and h-initial counters for reasons rooted in Old Japanese's own consonant inventory — the counter irregularities stop looking like an arbitrary list to memorize and start looking like the same one phonological story playing out in its last productive corner of the grammar.

title: Verb-final (SOV) word order and the head-final principle
explanation: Japanese consistently puts the verb last: subject, then object, then verb. This isn't just a quirk of one rule — Japanese is head-final throughout its grammar, which is also why descriptive clauses sit before the noun they modify and why particles follow nouns instead of coming before them like English prepositions.

examples.native: 私はりんごを食べます。
examples.gloss: I eat an apple. (literally: I apple eat)

examples.native: 田中さんは日本語を勉強します。
examples.gloss: Mr./Ms. Tanaka studies Japanese.

bridge_note: English fixes the verb in the middle of the sentence, right after the subject, so you know the action almost immediately. Japanese saves the verb for last, so you often can't tell what's actually happening — or whether the sentence is negative — until the very end.
mistake: Ordering words English-style (subject-verb-object) out of habit, which is simply ungrammatical in Japanese rather than just unnatural.
source: Genki I Lesson 1–2; standard typological description of Japanese
branch: Core Sentence Structure, the Copula & Particle Fundamentals
long_form:
Calling Japanese "SOV" is accurate but almost undersells the point, because the verb-final property isn't an isolated word-order fact sitting next to a pile of unrelated rules — it's the generative source of a huge amount of Japanese grammar that otherwise looks like a grab-bag of arbitrary quirks. Linguists describe Japanese as consistently head-final: in any phrase, the "head" (the word that determines what kind of phrase it is, and that governs the others) comes last, and everything that modifies or complements it comes before it. A verb is the head of a sentence, so the verb goes last, with its subject and object stacked in front of it in whatever order the speaker finds convenient (Japanese word order before the verb is actually fairly free, governed by particles rather than position — another consequence of not needing position to signal grammatical role the way English does). A noun is the head of a noun phrase, so anything describing that noun — an adjective, a possessive, or an entire relative clause — comes before it, never after. A postposition's "head" is the relationship it expresses, and the noun it attaches to comes before it, which is exactly why Japanese has postpositions (particles like に, で, を) trailing the noun instead of English-style prepositions leading it.

English is, by contrast, a fairly consistent head-initial language for phrases even though its clause-level word order (SVO) puts the verb in the middle — verbs precede their objects, prepositions precede their nouns, and while adjectives precede nouns (a quirk shared with Germanic languages generally), relative clauses trail behind ("the book that I bought," clause after noun). That single difference — modifying clause before the noun versus after it — is the single biggest source of disorientation for English-speaking intermediate learners, because parsing a Japanese sentence means holding an unresolved noun phrase in memory while a whole clause unspools in front of it, the mirror image of the English habit of hearing the noun first and only then finding out what modifies it.

The practical consequence that surprises learners most is what the short explanation calls out: because the verb comes last, and modifiers like negation and tense are suffixed onto that final verb, a Japanese sentence can run for a full breath without revealing whether it is affirmative or negative, past or present, a statement or a question — all of that information is withheld until the very last syllable. 田中さんは今日、会議に出席し… could still resolve as ません (didn't attend), ました (did attend), たいです (wants to attend), or ようとしています (is trying to attend), and a listener genuinely cannot commit to an interpretation until the verb complex finishes. This is sometimes cited (only half-jokingly) as a cultural explanation for why Japanese conversation tolerates listeners waiting attentively to the very end of an utterance rather than interrupting — whether or not that folk explanation holds up, the grammatical fact behind it is real and has no real parallel in English syntax.

It's worth being honest about the limits of head-finality as an organizing idea, though: it explains the order of major constituents and the direction relative clauses attach, but it does not, by itself, predict every detail of Japanese word order — topic-fronting (は) can pull a phrase to the very front of the sentence regardless of its grammatical role, and heavily head-final languages still vary in how rigidly they enforce the pattern. Treat "head-final" as the single best lens for understanding why so many seemingly unrelated Japanese structures (verb-last clauses, pre-nominal relative clauses, postpositions, adjectives before nouns) all point the same direction, not as a mechanical rule that generates every sentence on its own.

title: です/だ copula: "A is B" sentences
explanation: です (polite) and だ (plain) link a topic to a noun or na-adjective to say "A is B." Negation and past tense are built with fixed alternate forms rather than by conjugating です itself: negative じゃないです/ではありません, past でした/だった.

examples.native: 私は学生です。
examples.gloss: I am a student.

examples.native: 田中さんは先生じゃないです。
examples.gloss: Mr. Tanaka is not a teacher.

examples.native: 昨日は休みでした。
examples.gloss: Yesterday was a day off.

bridge_note: English "to be" conjugates for person and tense (am/is/are/was). Japanese です/だ don't change for person at all — only for politeness level, tense, and negation — because the person information is already carried by は and the topic noun.
mistake: Using です after an i-adjective and expecting it to carry the tense (高いでした ✗) — the adjective itself must conjugate; です there is politeness only.
branch: Core Sentence Structure, the Copula & Particle Fundamentals

title: は marks the topic ("as for X...")
explanation: は (pronounced "wa" only in this grammatical use) marks what the whole sentence is about — the topic — rather than necessarily the grammatical subject. Japanese is topic-prominent: the sentence is framed as a comment about something, and that something need not be the doer of the action.

examples.native: 私は学生です。
examples.gloss: As for me, (I) am a student.

examples.native: 象は鼻が長い。
examples.gloss: As for elephants, the trunk is long.

bridge_note: English is subject-prominent: every sentence needs one grammatical subject, and there's no separate slot for "the thing we're talking about" if it differs from the subject. Japanese can name a topic first and then a completely separate grammatical subject inside the comment about it.
mistake: Writing わ instead of は for the topic particle — they sound identical but は is spelled with the は kana whenever it's this grammatical marker.
branch: Core Sentence Structure, the Copula & Particle Fundamentals
long_form:
は does not mean "is" and it is not really a subject marker, even though every beginner course introduces it in sentences that make it look like one. What は actually does is set up a frame: it announces the thing the rest of the sentence is going to be a comment about, and then everything after it — including a full clause with its own grammatical subject — is offered as commentary on that frame. This is why 象は鼻が長い works at all: it does not mean "the elephant is a long nose," it means "as for elephants, [the] trunk is long," with 鼻 (trunk) sitting in as the actual grammatical subject of 長い inside the comment. English speakers stumble here because English has no separate slot for "the thing under discussion" apart from the grammatical subject — in English the subject has to do double duty as both agent and topic, so a sentence built the elephant way simply cannot be said without paraphrase ("elephants have long trunks," "as for elephants, their trunks are long").

The topic-prominent versus subject-prominent distinction is a genuine typological fault line among the world's languages, and Japanese sits firmly on the topic-prominent side along with Korean, Mandarin, and a scatter of other unrelated languages — it is not a Japanese-specific quirk but a whole different way of organizing what a sentence is "about." Historically は develops out of an Old Japanese binding particle used for contrast and emphasis, and that contrastive flavor never fully disappeared: even today, marking something with は inside a sentence that already has a topic (私はすしは好きです, "as for me, sushi [at least] I like") reliably signals "this one, as opposed to something else," which is one reason は can feel oddly pointed in a context where you only meant to be neutral.

The famous は/が confusion that every textbook warns about is really a symptom of this typological gap rather than a simple vocabulary mix-up. In a huge number of ordinary sentences — 私は学生です being the textbook example — the topic and the grammatical subject happen to be the exact same noun, so learners quietly absorb "は = subject" as a working rule that holds up fine until it suddenly doesn't: the moment topic and subject diverge, as in the elephant sentence, or the moment new information needs introducing (Unit 2's other particle, が, handles that job), the は-as-subject rule breaks down and has to be replaced with something closer to "は = what we already know we're discussing, marked as the frame." The spelling trap the entry flags — writing わ instead of は — is a much shallower issue than this, a historical leftover from an old kana-usage rule (the topic particle keeps its old orthographic spelling は even though it is pronounced wa), but it is worth knowing that the leftover exists specifically because は was frozen into a grammatical particle early enough in the language's history to escape a later spelling reform that regularized ordinary は/わ pronunciation elsewhere.

One nuance a short flashcard never has room for: は can mark a topic that isn't even present anywhere else in the sentence as a normal argument. 今日は雨だ ("as for today, it's raining") doesn't have "today" filling any object or location slot that a verb like 降る would otherwise need — 雨だ alone would be a complete sentence, and 今日は is purely scene-setting, glued on as a frame with no particular grammatical relationship to what follows beyond "this is what we're now discussing." Once you can hear は this way — not as a subject label but as a topic flag that can attach to almost anything, including a completely different sentence's leftover context — a lot of Japanese sentence structure that looks bizarrely front-loaded in early textbooks (long topic phrases stacked before a short comment) stops looking bizarre and starts looking like the single most natural way to organize information in this language.

title: が marks the subject, especially new information
explanation: が marks the grammatical subject of a sentence, and is especially used when introducing new or identifying information — answering an implicit "who?" or "what?". A rough rule of thumb: は = known theme ("as for X"), が = new information or the answer to a question word.

examples.native: 猫がいます。
examples.gloss: There is a cat. (introducing a cat as new information)

examples.native: 誰が来ましたか。
examples.gloss: Who came?

bridge_note: English uses a single word ("the subject") for both the sentence's topic and its grammatical agent, so the topic/subject distinction rarely needs marking. Japanese requires が (not は) whenever the subject is new, unknown, or being singled out — a distinction English speakers have to learn to hear.
mistake: Conflating は and が because in many simple sentences the topic and subject happen to be the same noun — が is nevertheless obligatory with existence verbs (ある/いる) and directly after question words like 誰 (who) or 何 (what).
branch: Core Sentence Structure, the Copula & Particle Fundamentals
long_form:
If は sets up what a sentence is about, が answers a much narrower question: who or what, specifically, is doing this or existing here — especially when that answer is new to the conversation. The clearest place to see が in its purest form is with the existence verbs ある/いる: 猫がいます doesn't have a topic at all, it's a flat assertion that a cat exists, and が is the only particle that can mark the thing being asserted into existence. The same logic explains why が is grammatically forced immediately after a question word — 誰が来ましたか cannot become 誰は来ましたか, because a question word is definitionally new information waiting to be filled in, and は's whole job is marking something already established as shared ground between speaker and listener. You cannot make already-known common ground out of the very blank you're asking someone to fill in.

This is worth dwelling on because English genuinely doesn't have this distinction anywhere in its grammar. English "the subject" is a single, undifferentiated grammatical role: whatever you conjugate the verb to agree with. It is completely indifferent to whether that noun is old information the listener already has in mind or brand-new information being introduced for the first time — English speakers signal that difference, if at all, with stress, word order tricks ("there's a cat" fronting with a dummy subject), or nothing at all. Japanese, by contrast, makes the new/given distinction structurally mandatory via は versus が, which means English speakers have to learn to actively listen for a distinction their own language never trained their ear to notice.

The rule of thumb the short explanation gives — は known theme, が new information or answer to a question word — is a genuinely good rule of thumb, but it undersells how often native speakers reach for が specifically to narrow down or single out one candidate among several possible subjects, which is a slightly different flavor of "new" than pure introduction. 誰が窓を開けましたか ("who opened the window?") followed by 田中さんが開けました ("[it was] Tanaka [who] opened it") uses が in the answer precisely because the sentence is functioning as an identifying statement — picking Tanaka out from a field of candidates — rather than a neutral comment about Tanaka as an already-established topic. If Tanaka had already been the topic of conversation, the natural answer would shift to は: 田中さんは開けませんでした ("Tanaka didn't open it," as a comment continuing to talk about Tanaka specifically). This exhaustive-versus-descriptive distinction (linguists sometimes call the が use here "exhaustive-listing") is one layer beyond what a beginner needs on day one, but it's the piece that explains why native speakers' は/が choices can feel unpredictable even after you've memorized every rule in the textbook: the choice tracks a real cognitive category — what's presupposed versus what's being asserted or singled out — not a fixed lexical pairing with particular verbs or nouns.

The practical trap for English speakers is exactly the one the short explanation names: in a huge fraction of ordinary sentences topic and subject are the same noun, so learners default to treating は and が as free variants and pick whichever one comes to mind first. The fix is not memorizing more sentence patterns but retraining the underlying question you ask yourself before choosing a particle — not "what's the subject of this sentence" but "is this noun something we're both already tracking, or am I introducing/identifying/singling it out right now?" Once that question becomes automatic, が's behavior with ある/いる and question words stops looking like an arbitrary grammar rule and starts looking like the single most predictable particle in the language.

title: を marks the direct object
explanation: を follows a noun to mark it as the direct object of the verb that follows — the thing being acted on. It's pronounced simply "o" despite the extra kana shape.

examples.native: りんごを食べます。
examples.gloss: I eat an apple.

examples.native: 本を読みます。
examples.gloss: I read a book.

bridge_note: English marks the object purely by word order (it comes right after the verb). Japanese marks it explicitly with を regardless of where it sits relative to the verb, which is what allows Japanese word order to stay flexible for emphasis while roles stay clear.
mistake: Omitting を and relying on word order the way English does, which is grammatical only in very casual speech where context makes the object obvious.
branch: Core Sentence Structure, the Copula & Particle Fundamentals

title: に vs で: existence/destination/time vs. location of action
explanation: に marks a static location of existence, a destination, or a point in time; で marks the location where an action takes place, or the means/instrument used. Mixing these two up is one of the most common beginner errors because English "at/in" covers both jobs with one word.

examples.native: 公園に猫がいます。
examples.gloss: There is a cat in the park. (static existence → に)

examples.native: 図書館で勉強します。
examples.gloss: I study at the library. (location of an action → で)

examples.native: バスで行きます。
examples.gloss: I go by bus. (means → で)

bridge_note: English "at/in" doesn't distinguish between where something simply exists and where an action happens — both are just "at the library." Japanese forces that distinction onto the particle every time, which is exactly why it's a persistent error for English speakers.
mistake: 図書館に勉強する (using に for the location of an action) instead of the correct 図書館で勉強する — a very common transfer error from English "at."
branch: Core Sentence Structure, the Copula & Particle Fundamentals

title: へ marks direction toward a goal
explanation: へ (pronounced "e" in this use, not "he") marks the direction of movement, overlapping heavily with destination に but putting more emphasis on the direction/goal of travel itself rather than the endpoint as a fact.

examples.native: 日本へ行きます。
examples.gloss: I'm going to Japan.

examples.native: どちらへ？
examples.gloss: Where are you headed? (casual, friendly way to ask)

bridge_note: English uses "to" for both plain destination and directional movement without distinguishing them. Japanese has two overlapping particles (に and へ) here, and beginners can treat them as interchangeable with 行く-type verbs without being wrong.
mistake: Confusing へ (direction, pronounced "e") with へ read as "he" — this is the one kana whose pronunciation changes specifically in this grammatical role.
branch: Core Sentence Structure, the Copula & Particle Fundamentals

title: の links nouns: possession and description
explanation: の connects two nouns, most often to show possession ("my book") but also general noun-to-noun description, and can chain multiple times in a row.

examples.native: 私の本
examples.gloss: my book

examples.native: 日本語の先生
examples.gloss: a Japanese-language teacher (literally: Japanese-language's teacher)

bridge_note: English marks possession with 's or "of," and switches word order between the two ("my friend's book" vs "the book of my friend"). Japanese の always works the same single way, in the same head-final order (possessor + の + possessed), no matter how many nouns are chained together.
mistake: Dropping の between two nouns the way English can drop "of" in compounds ("coffee cup") — Japanese needs の explicitly linking them almost every time.
branch: Core Sentence Structure, the Copula & Particle Fundamentals

title: と vs や: exhaustive vs. partial listing
explanation: と lists items exhaustively ("A and B, and that's everything"), while や lists a few representative examples out of a larger unstated set ("A, B, among other things").

examples.native: りんごとみかんを買いました。
examples.gloss: I bought an apple and a mandarin orange. (only those two things, full stop)

examples.native: りんごやみかんを買いました。
examples.gloss: I bought things like apples and mandarin oranges. (and maybe other fruit too)

bridge_note: English "and" is exhaustive by default, and "or something like that" has to be tacked on separately to signal a partial list. Japanese builds that exhaustive/partial distinction directly into which listing particle you choose.
mistake: Using と when a partial, illustrative list was meant, which unintentionally claims the list is complete.
branch: Core Sentence Structure, the Copula & Particle Fundamentals

title: も "also/too" replaces は/が/を
explanation: も means "also" or "too," and it replaces は, が, or を on the noun it attaches to rather than stacking alongside them.

examples.native: 私も学生です。
examples.gloss: I am also a student.

examples.native: お茶もください。
examples.gloss: Please give me tea too.

bridge_note: English adds "too" or "also" as an extra word without touching the sentence's existing structure. Japanese instead swaps the particle itself for も — you can't say は...も or を...も together for the same noun.
mistake: Keeping は or を alongside も (私はも学生です ✗) instead of letting も fully replace it.
branch: Core Sentence Structure, the Copula & Particle Fundamentals

title: から/まで: "from/until" for time and place
explanation: から marks a starting point and まで marks an ending point, for both time and physical distance, and the two are often used together as a pair.

examples.native: 月曜日から金曜日まで働きます。
examples.gloss: I work from Monday until Friday.

examples.native: 駅から家まで歩きます。
examples.gloss: I walk from the station to my house.

bridge_note: English relative time words like "today" or "tomorrow" never take a preposition ("I'll go today," not "I'll go on today"). Japanese relative time words behave the same way — they take no particle at all, which trips up learners who expect に by analogy with clock times.
mistake: 今日に行きます (adding に to a relative time word) instead of the correct particle-less 今日行きます.
branch: Core Sentence Structure, the Copula & Particle Fundamentals

title: か turns a statement into a yes/no question
explanation: Adding か to the end of a sentence turns it into a yes/no question, with no change to word order and no auxiliary verb needed.

examples.native: 学生ですか。
examples.gloss: Are you a student?

examples.native: 日本語がわかりますか。
examples.gloss: Do you understand Japanese?

bridge_note: English inverts subject and auxiliary to ask a question ("You are" → "Are you...?"). Japanese marks the question purely morphologically, with a single particle at the end, so the rest of the sentence never has to move.
mistake: Trying to invert word order or insert a "do"-equivalent auxiliary the way English does — Japanese needs neither; just append か.
branch: Core Sentence Structure, the Copula & Particle Fundamentals

title: ある/いる: two existence verbs, animate vs. inanimate
explanation: Japanese uses two completely different verbs for "there is/are" depending on whether the subject is animate (いる: people, animals) or inanimate (ある: objects, plants, abstract things).

examples.native: 猫がいます。
examples.gloss: There is a cat.

examples.native: 机の上に本があります。
examples.gloss: There is a book on the desk.

bridge_note: English "there is/are" doesn't care whether the subject is alive. Japanese splits existence into two verbs along the animate/inanimate line, so choosing the wrong one is a grammar error, not just a stylistic slip.
mistake: Using ある for people or animals (猫があります ✗) — animate beings always take いる.

title: I-adjectives conjugate like verbs
explanation: Adjectives ending in い (i-adjectives) carry their own tense and negation, conjugating the adjective itself rather than needing a separate "to be" verb to change. です after an i-adjective adds only politeness, never tense.

examples.native: このケーキは高いです。
examples.gloss: This cake is expensive.

examples.native: このケーキは高かったです。
examples.gloss: This cake was expensive.

examples.native: このケーキは高くないです。
examples.gloss: This cake isn't expensive.

bridge_note: English adjectives never change form — tense always comes from a separate "was/is." I-adjectives are historically verb-like in Japanese and inflect on their own, which is why 高いでした is simply wrong; the correct past is 高かったです.
mistake: Saying 高いでした instead of 高かったです — です cannot carry past tense for an i-adjective; the adjective ending itself must change to かった.

title: Na-adjectives behave like nouns
explanation: The second adjective class (na-adjectives) behaves grammatically like a noun: it needs な inserted before a noun it modifies, and uses だ/です as its copula for tense and negation, just like です/だ sentences do.

examples.native: 静かな部屋
examples.gloss: a quiet room

examples.native: この部屋は静かじゃないです。
examples.gloss: This room isn't quiet.

examples.native: 昨日は静かだった。
examples.gloss: It was quiet yesterday.

bridge_note: English treats all adjectives the same way regardless of origin. Japanese na-adjectives are historically noun-like, so they conjugate through the copula (だ/です) exactly like a noun sentence would, never taking the i-adjective's く/かった endings.
mistake: Conjugating a na-adjective like an i-adjective (静かくない ✗ instead of 静かじゃない), or forgetting the な before a following noun (静か部屋 ✗ instead of 静かな部屋).

title: 好き・嫌い・上手・下手 take が, not を
explanation: Words like 好き (like), 嫌い (dislike), 上手 (good at), and 下手 (bad at) are grammatically na-adjectives, and the thing being liked, disliked, or skilled-at is marked with が, not を, even though the English translation feels like a direct object.

examples.native: 私は寿司が好きです。
examples.gloss: I like sushi.

examples.native: 彼女はピアノが上手です。
examples.gloss: She's good at piano.

bridge_note: English "I like sushi" treats "sushi" as the direct object of the verb "like." Japanese 好きです isn't a verb at all — it's an adjective describing the speaker, and the thing being liked is grammatically more like the subject of "is likeable to me," which is why it takes が.
mistake: Marking the liked/skilled-at thing with を (寿司を好きです ✗) by directly transferring English's "like + object" pattern.

title: Counters and classifiers for numbers
explanation: Japanese doesn't attach a number directly to a noun the way English does — it inserts a classifier word chosen by the shape or category of what's being counted (long thin objects, flat objects, small animals, people, and so on), and the number itself often changes sound when combined with certain counters.

examples.native: ペンが三本あります。
examples.gloss: There are three pens. (三本 for long, thin objects)

examples.native: 猫が二匹います。
examples.gloss: There are two cats. (二匹 for small animals)

examples.native: 一人、二人、三人
examples.gloss: one person, two people, three people (hitori, futari use native readings; sannin onward is regular).

bridge_note: English generally counts nouns directly ("three pens") and only reaches for a classifier with mass nouns ("two sheets of paper"). Japanese requires a classifier for essentially every countable noun, and the number+counter combination often shifts sound (一本 ippon, 三本 sanbon, 六本 roppon) via the same rendaku/gemination pattern from the writing-system unit, concentrated around 1, 3, 6, 8, and 10.
mistake: Using the generic counter つ (hitotsu, futatsu...) for everything instead of learning the object-specific counter, or forgetting that 一人/二人 use irregular native readings while 三人 onward switches to the regular Sino-Japanese numbers.

title: これ/それ/あれ/どれ and この/その/あの/どの: the kosoado system
explanation: Japanese demonstratives split into a three-way proximal/medial/distal system rather than English's two-way this/that: これ/この = near the speaker, それ/その = near the listener, あれ/あの = far from both. どれ/どの are the question-word forms ("which").

examples.native: これは私の本です。
examples.gloss: This is my book. (near me)

examples.native: それはあなたの本ですか。
examples.gloss: Is that your book? (near you)

examples.native: あの人は先生です。
examples.gloss: That person over there is a teacher. (far from both of us)

bridge_note: English collapses distance into just "this" (near me) and "that" (not near me), with no dedicated word for "near you specifically." Japanese keeps that middle ground as its own category, giving a three-way spatial logic English speakers have to consciously build.
mistake: Using これ/この for something near the listener instead of それ/その, by mentally mapping Japanese's three-way system onto English's two-way this/that.

title: The three verb groups (godan, ichidan, irregular)
explanation: Every Japanese verb belongs to one of three conjugation groups, and this classification governs every later conjugation rule: Group 1 (godan/u-verbs, e.g. 書く, 飲む, 話す) cycle through all five vowel grades; Group 2 (ichidan/ru-verbs, e.g. 食べる, 見る) conjugate on a single vowel grade; Group 3 (irregular: する, 来る) follow their own patterns entirely.

examples.native: 書く (godan)
examples.gloss: to write — stem shifts through ka/ki/ku/ke/ko.

examples.native: 食べる (ichidan)
examples.gloss: to eat — stem stays on "tabe-" for every conjugation.

examples.native: する / 来る (irregular)
examples.gloss: to do / to come — each conjugates in its own unique way.

bridge_note: English has only a handful of truly irregular verbs (be, go, have) and otherwise conjugates fairly uniformly. Japanese requires sorting every single verb into one of three groups before you can conjugate it at all, because the te-form, potential form, and every other later form depend entirely on which group a verb belongs to.
mistake: Misclassifying "impostor" verbs that look like ichidan (end in -eru/-iru) but are actually godan — 帰る (kaeru, "to return"), 走る (hashiru, "to run"), 切る (kiru, "to cut") — which must simply be memorized, since misclassifying them breaks every conjugation built on top.
branch: Verb Groups & the Polite (ます) Form

title: ます-form: polite present and past
explanation: The ます form is the standard polite conjugation for present/future and past, in both affirmative and negative, and is the safe default register for strangers, coworkers, and most public situations.

examples.native: 毎日日本語を勉強します。
examples.gloss: I study Japanese every day.

examples.native: 昨日は勉強しませんでした。
examples.gloss: I didn't study yesterday.

bridge_note: English doesn't grammaticalize politeness into the verb itself — "study" is the same word whether you're speaking to a boss or a close friend. Japanese ます endings exist purely to encode formal register, on top of (not instead of) tense and negation.
mistake: Forgetting that ます itself doesn't tell you the verb's underlying group — the ます-stem shortcut for forming other conjugations only reliably works for ichidan verbs, not godan.
branch: Verb Groups & the Polite (ます) Form

title: ましょう/ませんか: invitations
explanation: ましょう proposes an action together ("let's..."), while ませんか asks the same thing as a softer, more considerate question ("won't you...?"), leaving more room for the listener to decline.

examples.native: 一緒に行きましょう。
examples.gloss: Let's go together.

examples.native: 一緒に行きませんか。
examples.gloss: Won't you come with me? / Would you like to go together?

bridge_note: English "let's" is a single fixed phrase with no built-in politeness gradient. Japanese offers two distinct invitation forms at different politeness levels, letting the speaker choose how much they're presuming the listener's agreement.
mistake: Treating ましょう and ませんか as fully interchangeable — ませんか is noticeably more polite and less presumptuous, and is generally preferred when inviting someone you don't know well.
branch: Verb Groups & the Polite (ます) Form

title: The agglutinative principle: verbs built by gluing suffixes
explanation: Japanese verb forms are built by gluing suffixes onto a stem in a fixed, predictable order (stem + causative + passive + aspect + politeness + tense), rather than by memorizing each combination as its own irregular form. Recognizing this pattern early makes even the scariest-looking later forms (like the causative-passive) decomposable rather than something to memorize wholesale.

examples.native: 食べ + させ + られ + ました
examples.gloss: was made to eat (politely, in the past) — stem + causative + passive + past-polite, glued in order.

examples.native: 食べ + ます
examples.gloss: eat (politely) — the simplest case of the same gluing principle.

bridge_note: English builds equivalent meanings with separate helper words in a chain ("was made to eat" uses three separate words). Japanese fuses the same meanings into one continuous verb by stacking suffixes onto a single stem, in a strict and learnable order.
mistake: Treating each new complex verb form (causative, passive, causative-passive) as an entirely new thing to memorize, instead of recognizing it as the same familiar stem with one more suffix glued on.
source: General agglutinative-morphology framing; not a specific citable textbook rule
branch: Verb Groups & the Polite (ます) Form
long_form:
Once a learner has survived verb groups, the ます-form, and a first brush with plain form, Japanese verb morphology can start to feel like an ever-expanding pile of forms to memorize independently — te-form, potential, causative, passive, causative-passive, each with its own conjugation table. The single most useful conceptual reframe available at this stage is realizing that none of these are actually independent forms at all: they are all instances of one mechanical process, gluing a fixed inventory of meaningful suffixes onto a stem in a strict, predictable order, the way you might snap together modular building blocks rather than memorizing a new word from scratch each time. This is what "agglutinative" means as a linguistic typology label, and Japanese is a textbook example of the type, standing in the same broad structural family as Turkish, Korean, Finnish, and Swahili — languages where grammatical meaning accumulates through a sequence of clearly segmentable suffixes, each contributing one discrete piece of meaning, rather than fusing multiple meanings into a single unanalyzable ending the way, say, Latin or Spanish verb conjugations often do (Spanish hablé packs person, number, tense, and aspect into one indivisible ending; Japanese 話しました keeps "polite" and "past" as separately identifiable, individually swappable pieces: 話します, 話しました, 話しませんでした, each a different, separately meaningful suffix stacked in the same slot).

English, for contrast, is only mildly agglutinative and mostly analytic instead — English tends to express grammatical meaning through separate helper words (will, have, been, was) surrounding a largely unchanging main verb, rather than through suffixes piling onto the verb itself. "He was made to eat" strings together five separate words, each doing one job, none of them fused onto "eat" morphologically. Japanese does the equivalent work by fusing everything directly onto the verb stem in sequence: 食べさせられました stacks causative (させ) then passive (られ) then polite (まし) then past (た) onto 食べ, four distinct pieces of meaning, four historically separate morphemes, glued in a fixed pipeline order that never varies regardless of which verb you start with. Once you can see the seams — 食べ-させ-られ-まし-た — a form that looks intimidating as a single five-syllable word becomes trivially decomposable into pieces you already individually know.

The reason the curriculum introduces this idea explicitly, right after the polite ます-form and before plain form and the te-form's explosion of downstream uses, is entirely pedagogical rather than just linguistically tidy: naming the pipeline now means that every subsequent "scary" verb form the learner meets later — potential, passive, causative, and eventually their combination — can be met with the reaction "another suffix in the known slot order" rather than "an entirely new form to memorize from zero." The order itself is genuinely fixed and worth internalizing as a structure, not just a vague impression: stem, then voice-changing suffixes (causative and/or passive, in that order if both appear), then aspect markers if present, then the politeness layer (ます or its absence), then tense. A learner who has this template can predict, before ever seeing 飲まされていました in a textbook, roughly what shape it should take and what each piece should mean, purely from knowing the pipeline and the individual suffixes already covered — which is a fundamentally different, faster way of acquiring new-looking verb forms than treating each one as an isolated vocabulary item to be drilled independently.

The limits of the idea are worth naming too, so it isn't oversold: agglutination describes verb (and adjective) morphology specifically, not the whole grammar — particle choice, word order, and register are governed by separate systems this principle doesn't touch, and a small number of forms (the irregular verbs する/来る, and true exceptions like 行って) don't decompose as cleanly as the regular pipeline would predict, requiring memorization exactly the way any language's irregular forms do. But as a lens for the specific, notoriously long verb chains Japanese is famous for — the ones that look impossible to an English speaker seeing them cold — agglutination is the single idea that turns "memorize this whole word" into "recognize five pieces you already know, in an order you already know," which is as close as Japanese conjugation gets to actually getting easier the further into the curriculum you go, rather than harder.

title: Plain non-past (dictionary form)
explanation: The plain non-past, also called the dictionary form, is the form verbs are listed under in dictionaries and the base every other conjugation (te-form, past, potential) is built from. It expresses present/future in casual speech.

examples.native: 毎日日本語を勉強する。
examples.gloss: I study Japanese every day. (casual register)

examples.native: 明日、友達に会う。
examples.gloss: I'm meeting a friend tomorrow.

bridge_note: English doesn't have a single "citation form" that a whole grammar system builds from in the same way — the base form and the casual present tense happen to look alike by coincidence ("I eat"). In Japanese the dictionary form is deliberately also the casual present, and nearly every subordinate clause attaches to this plain form rather than to the polite ます form.
mistake: Assuming plain form is only for looking words up in a dictionary and never realizing it's also the actual casual-speech present tense used with friends and family.

title: Plain negative: the ない-form
explanation: The plain negative (ない-form) is built by shifting a godan verb's final vowel to the a-row before adding ない (書く→書かない), or dropping る and adding ない for ichidan verbs (食べる→食べない); ある is irregular, becoming ない itself rather than あらない.

examples.native: 今日は勉強しない。
examples.gloss: I'm not studying today. (casual)

examples.native: 肉を食べない。
examples.gloss: I don't eat meat.

bridge_note: English negates with a separate helper word ("don't/doesn't") in front of the verb. Japanese instead reshapes the verb's own ending into a negative adjective-like form (ない, which itself conjugates like an i-adjective), fusing negation into the verb rather than adding a word beside it.
mistake: Forgetting that ある's negative is the irregular ない, not あらない — the one true irregularity in an otherwise very regular pattern.

title: Plain past: the た-form
explanation: The plain past (た-form) uses the exact same sound-change rules as the te-form, just swapping the final て/で for た/だ — so 食べる→食べた, 書く→書いた. Mastering one form gives you the other for free.

examples.native: 昨日、映画を見た。
examples.gloss: I watched a movie yesterday. (casual)

examples.native: 手紙を書いた。
examples.gloss: I wrote a letter.

bridge_note: English forms the past tense with its own separate rule (often just "-ed," unrelated to any other verb form). Japanese's plain past reuses the identical stem sound-changes as the te-form, so the two forms are learned essentially as one system with two different endings.
mistake: Learning the te-form and た-form sound changes as two unrelated things to memorize twice, instead of recognizing they're the same stem change with a different final consonant.
source: Genki I Lesson 8 (shares Lesson 6 te-form sound changes)

title: Plain past negative
explanation: The plain past negative conjugates the ない-form the same way an i-adjective conjugates into its own past (ない→なかった), giving all four plain-form tenses once combined with the earlier three.

examples.native: 昨日は勉強しなかった。
examples.gloss: I didn't study yesterday.

examples.native: 肉を食べなかった。
examples.gloss: I didn't eat meat.

bridge_note: English builds this tense with two separate helper words ("didn't") that don't otherwise conjugate. Japanese instead conjugates ない itself into its past form (なかった) exactly like any other i-adjective would, keeping the whole negative-past system internally consistent.
mistake: Trying to conjugate なかった as if it were a separate irregular ending, rather than recognizing it as ない simply taking the regular i-adjective past ending (い→かった).

title: When to use ます vs. plain form
explanation: ます register is used with strangers, superiors, and in public contexts; plain form is used with family and close friends, and — critically — inside essentially all embedded/subordinate clauses regardless of how polite the overall sentence is. Register choice encodes the same in-group/out-group social awareness (uchi/soto) that later governs keigo and giving-and-receiving verbs.

examples.native: 友達と話すとき、丁寧語は使わない。
examples.gloss: When talking with friends, I don't use polite language. (plain form used inside the subordinate とき clause even though the main sentence could be polite)

examples.native: 先生が来ると思います。
examples.gloss: I think the teacher is coming. (plain 来る inside the と思います clause, ます only on the outer verb)

bridge_note: English formality is a matter of word choice and tone ("grab a bite" vs. "would you care to dine"), not a grammatical requirement tied to sentence structure. Japanese requires plain form inside subordinate clauses as a hard grammatical rule, independent of how polite the speaker is being overall — stacking ます inside an embedded clause is simply ungrammatical, not just overly formal.
mistake: Using plain form as the main predicate with a social superior (comes across as rude), or the mirror-image error of stacking ます inside a relative or subordinate clause where only plain form is grammatical.

title: Te-form conjugation: the pedagogical hinge
explanation: The te-form is a non-finite connector shape every verb has, with sound changes depending on the verb group and, for godan verbs, the final consonant: ichidan drops る and adds て (食べる→食べて); godan changes by ending — く→いて (書く→書いて), ぐ→いで (泳ぐ→泳いで), う/つ/る→って (買う→買って), ぬ/ぶ/む→んで (飲む→飲んで), す→して (話す→話して); irregular する→して, 来る→来て. One key exception: 行く→行って, not the expected 行いて.

examples.native: 食べて
examples.gloss: eating / and eat (te-form of 食べる)

examples.native: 書いて
examples.gloss: writing / and write (te-form of 書く)

examples.native: 行って
examples.gloss: going / and go — the one irregular exception to the く→いて rule.

bridge_note: English has no equivalent single connector form — it just repeats "and" between verbs. The te-form's sound changes are the single most memorized rule in beginner Japanese because it unlocks requests, permission, prohibition, and the entire aspect system covered in the next unit.
mistake: Applying the ます-stem shortcut for forming the te-form, which happens to work for ichidan verbs but produces the wrong result for every godan verb.
source: Genki I Lesson 6 (te-form introduced here; well-corroborated against Genki's official lesson sequence)
long_form:
No single conjugation rule in beginner Japanese carries more downstream weight than the te-form, and it's worth understanding why before drilling the sound changes themselves. The te-form is what linguists call a non-finite connective form: unlike every other verb form covered up to this point in the curriculum, it carries no tense of its own and cannot stand alone as the final predicate of a sentence. Its entire job is to link — to a following clause (て-form sequencing, "get up, eat, and go"), to a following helper verb (くれる, いる, ある, しまう, おく — each attaching to the te-form to build a whole family of grammaticalized meanings), or to a fixed set phrase (てください, てもいい, てはいけない). Tense, when it matters, is carried entirely by whatever comes after the te-form, or by the final verb in a chain — which is exactly why 起きて、食べて、行きます works: only 行きます is finite, and it retroactively supplies tense for the whole sequence.

The sound changes themselves (く→いて, ぐ→いで, う/つ/る→って, ぬ/ぶ/む→んで, す→して for godan verbs; drop る and add て for ichidan; irregular する→して and 来る→来て) are not arbitrary memorization fodder — they are the exact same historical sound-change family, euphonic consonant assimilation, that produced the past-tense た-form changes in Unit 5 and the sound shifts behind rendaku and counter irregularities back in Unit 1. Old Japanese verb endings underwent regular phonetic erosion and assimilation as the language evolved toward its modern form, and the te-form and た-form happen to be the two places where that erosion is most visible and most systematized today — which is also exactly why they pattern identically (書いて/書いた, 飲んで/飲んだ): once you know one, you effectively already know the other, since they're the same historical sound change wearing two different grammatical hats.

The one true irregularity, 行く→行って (not the expected 行いて), is worth pausing on precisely because it's presented as an exception to memorize rather than explained, and the honest answer is that it's a genuine historical irregularity rather than a rule you're failing to see: 行く underwent a slightly different, non-productive sound change than the rest of the く-ending verb class, for reasons rooted in its own particular historical development rather than a a general pattern you can extend to other verbs. It sits alongside a very small number of other true irregular te-forms in the same category, which is precisely why every Japanese textbook flags it individually instead of trying to fold it into the general く→いて rule.

The mistake called out in the short explanation — the ます-stem shortcut (drop ます, add て) — deserves a fuller diagnosis because it's such a natural trap: the shortcut genuinely does work for every ichidan verb (食べます→食べて, たしかに just drop the stem-final vowel and add て) precisely because ichidan te-form formation is itself just "drop る, add て," which happens to align with the ます-stem. For godan verbs, though, the ます-stem (書きます, 飲みます, 話します) strips away exactly the final-consonant information that determines which of the five godan sound changes applies — く versus ぐ versus す versus the merged う/つ/る group are indistinguishable once you're looking only at the ます-stem, so a learner relying on that shortcut for a godan verb is, in effect, throwing away the one piece of information they need and then guessing. The fix isn't a better shortcut — it's accepting that godan te-form formation genuinely requires knowing the verb's original dictionary-form ending, which is exactly the discipline the whole verb-groups unit (Unit 4) was building toward in the first place. English has no equivalent connector form at all — English simply repeats "and" between every clause ("I got up, and I ate, and I went") with each verb independently carrying its own tense — which is one more reason the te-form takes real, deliberate drilling for English speakers: there's no existing mental category in their native grammar to slot it into.

title: て-form for sequencing actions
explanation: Chaining several actions together in order uses the te-form on every verb except the last, which carries the sentence's actual tense; English's repeated "and" becomes a string of te-forms instead.

examples.native: 朝起きて、顔を洗って、朝ごはんを食べます。
examples.gloss: I get up, wash my face, and eat breakfast. (only the final verb, 食べます, is fully conjugated for tense)

bridge_note: English repeats "and" between each verb in a sequence and marks tense on all of them individually ("I got up and washed and ate"). Japanese shifts every verb but the last into the tenseless te-form, with tense carried only once, at the very end.
mistake: Fully conjugating every verb in the sequence for tense instead of leaving all but the final one in te-form.

title: てください: polite requests
explanation: Attaching ください to the te-form makes a polite request or instruction — "please do X" — and is one of the first practical uses of the te-form a learner can produce.

examples.native: ここに名前を書いてください。
examples.gloss: Please write your name here.

examples.native: ちょっと待ってください。
examples.gloss: Please wait a moment.

bridge_note: English "please" attaches to the bare verb ("please write"). Japanese instead requires the verb to first take its non-finite te-form before ください can attach — the request is built from a connector shape, not the dictionary form.
mistake: Attaching ください to the dictionary or ます form instead of the te-form (書くください ✗ / 書きますください ✗ instead of 書いてください).

title: てもいい(です): asking or giving permission
explanation: Te-form + もいいです asks or grants permission — "is it okay if..." / "you may..." — with か added to turn it into a yes/no question.

examples.native: ここで写真を撮ってもいいですか。
examples.gloss: May I take a photo here?

examples.native: はい、撮ってもいいです。
examples.gloss: Yes, you may take one.

bridge_note: English permission phrasing ("may I," "is it okay if") uses a modal verb up front. Japanese builds permission compositionally from the te-form plus "even if it's good," a literal structure ("even doing X is fine") quite different from English's modal-first approach.
mistake: Using てもいいです for a command/instruction rather than a genuine request for permission — it specifically frames the action as optional/allowed, not required.

title: てはいけない: prohibition
explanation: Te-form + はいけない (or the more polite いけません) states that an action is forbidden — the mirror-image counterpart to てもいい permission.

examples.native: ここで写真を撮ってはいけません。
examples.gloss: You must not take photos here.

examples.native: 教室で食べてはいけない。
examples.gloss: You can't eat in the classroom.

bridge_note: English prohibition uses "must not" or "can't," a single modal construction. Japanese again builds it compositionally from the te-form, literally "even doing X is no good" — the same building block (te-form + も/は + evaluative predicate) that also produces permission, just with は and a negative evaluation instead of いい.
mistake: Confusing てはいけない (forbidden) with ないほうがいい ("better not to," a softer suggestion) — the former is a hard prohibition, the latter just advice.

title: ている introduced as a te-form use
explanation: て-form + いる marks an action as ongoing at this point it's first introduced as one more thing the te-form connects to; the fuller aspectual system (progressive vs. resultative, habitual use) is developed in the next unit.

examples.native: 今、ご飯を食べています。
examples.gloss: I'm eating right now.

examples.native: 雨が降っています。
examples.gloss: It's raining.

bridge_note: English marks ongoing action with its own dedicated "-ing" verb ending, unrelated to any other grammar. Japanese instead builds it from the same te-form connector already used for requests and sequencing, plus いる ("to exist/be") — ongoing action is literally "existing in the state of having done X."
mistake: Treating ている as a totally separate form to memorize, rather than recognizing it as just another combination built on the te-form already learned.
source: Genki I Lesson 6 (introduced here; expanded in Lesson 7)

title: から: giving a reason with the plain form
explanation: から attached to a plain-form clause gives a reason ("because..."), and is deliberately contrasted here with the te-form: the te-form connects two actions/states neutrally with no causal claim, while から explicitly marks cause-and-effect.

examples.native: 忙しいから、行けません。
examples.gloss: Because I'm busy, I can't go.

examples.native: 疲れたから、早く寝ます。
examples.gloss: Because I'm tired, I'll go to bed early.

bridge_note: English "because" attaches to a full clause with no register restriction. Japanese から attaches to the plain form of the preceding clause (even in an otherwise polite sentence, the から-clause itself is typically plain), and is a genuine causal claim rather than the neutral, causally-agnostic linking the te-form provides.
mistake: Using the te-form where a real cause-and-effect reason is meant (て just links neutrally; it doesn't assert causation the way から does), or attaching から to a ます-form verb when plain form is expected inside the clause.

title: ている: progressive (action in progress)
explanation: With ongoing-process verbs, ている describes an action currently in progress — the closest Japanese equivalent to English's "-ing" continuous tense.

examples.native: 今、宿題をしています。
examples.gloss: I'm doing homework right now.

examples.native: 彼は走っています。
examples.gloss: He is running.

bridge_note: This is the one use of ている that maps cleanly onto English "-ing." The mismatch appears with a different class of verbs (covered next), which is exactly why Japanese aspect isn't simply "add ている and translate as -ing" across the board.
mistake: Assuming ている always means "-ing" and never checking whether the verb is a punctual change-of-state verb, which instead triggers the resultative reading covered next.
branch: Aspect: ている and Related States

title: ている: resultative state with change-of-state verbs
explanation: With punctual change-of-state verbs (verbs describing an instantaneous event rather than a drawn-out process), ている marks the resulting state after that event, not the event happening right now — 結婚している means "is married," not "is getting married."

examples.native: 田中さんは結婚しています。
examples.gloss: Mr. Tanaka is married.

examples.native: 彼は死んでいます。
examples.gloss: He is dead.

examples.native: ドアが開いています。
examples.gloss: The door is open.

bridge_note: English "-ing" always implies an action still in progress, so it's tempting to read 結婚している as "is getting married" or 知っている as "am knowing." Verbs like 死ぬ (to die) and 結婚する (to marry) describe a single instantaneous event, so their ている describes the lasting state that event left behind, not the event itself recurring or continuing.
mistake: Reading 知っている as "am knowing" (English doesn't even allow progressive "know") or translating 結婚している as "is getting married" instead of the correct "is married."
source: Genki I Lesson 7 (explicitly teaches "Motion Verbs + ている for Resulting State"; well-corroborated against Genki's official lesson content)
branch: Aspect: ている and Related States
long_form:
English speakers learn ている as "the progressive," the Japanese equivalent of "-ing," and that mapping works fine for exactly the kind of durative verb English also treats as an ongoing process: 食べている, "is eating," lines up cleanly with its English translation because both languages are describing a stretched-out activity captured mid-occurrence. The trouble starts with a specific class of verbs — punctual, change-of-state verbs describing a single instantaneous transition rather than a process with duration — where Japanese and English aspect systems quietly diverge, and 結婚している is the textbook case: 結婚する describes the momentary event of getting married, the wedding itself, not an ongoing process, so ている attached to it cannot mean "is in the process of that momentary event" (that would be a contradiction — the event is instantaneous, it has no middle to be caught in). Instead ている shifts to marking the state that persists after the event completed: "is married," the resultant condition, not the transition into it. The same logic explains 死んでいる ("is dead," the lasting state after the punctual event of dying, never "is dying" — that meaning requires the different, unrelated construction 死にかけている) and ドアが開いている ("the door is open," the resulting state after someone or something opened it, as opposed to the door being mid-swing).

The deep reason this happens is that ている is not really "the progressive" at all — it's better understood as a general marker of an ongoing relevant state connected to a prior event, and which flavor of state it produces (ongoing action-in-progress, or lasting result-of-a-completed-event) is predictable from the verb's own inherent aspectual class, not from ている itself. Durative verbs (食べる, 読む, 書く — activities with real internal duration) yield the progressive reading; punctual/telic verbs (死ぬ, 結婚する, 開く, 来る) yield the resultative reading, because there's no meaningful "middle" of an instantaneous event for progressive aspect to describe. This is a genuine linguistic universal that shows up (with different surface machinery) across many languages' aspect systems, not a Japanese idiosyncrasy — but English happens to handle the punctual/durative distinction very differently, largely by choosing different verb forms or paraphrases rather than reusing one marker for both, which is exactly why English speakers don't come in with the right intuition already built.

This is also precisely why 知っている trips up nearly every English-speaking learner at some point: 知る is a punctual verb meaning "to come to know / to learn (a fact)," not an ongoing state-of-knowing verb the way English "to know" is — English simply doesn't distinguish "the momentary event of learning something" from "the ongoing state of knowing it," using the single verb "know" (stative, no natural progressive) for both. Japanese does distinguish them: 知る names the punctual event, and 知っている is its resultative — the state that persists after you learned the fact, i.e., "I know [it]." Reading 知っている as "am knowing" is a category error baked in by assuming ている always means progressive; the fix is realizing 知る itself never means "to know" in the English stative sense at all, only "to find out/learn," so ている is doing exactly the same resultative job here that it does with 結婚する and 死ぬ.

A nuance worth adding beyond what a short card can hold: this progressive/resultative split isn't a closed, memorize-the-list system — a handful of verbs are genuinely ambiguous depending on context, and some verbs pattern with one reading in isolation but shift depending on whether they're used transitively or intransitively (compare 電気をつけている, someone currently in the act of turning a light on, versus 電気がついている, the light is currently in the on state as a result of having been turned on — the transitive/intransitive pairing from Unit 13 interacts directly with which ている reading surfaces). The practical takeaway for a learner is to stop asking "what does ている mean" as if it had one fixed translation, and start asking "is this verb describing a process with real duration, or an instantaneous transition" — once that question becomes reflexive, ている's apparent inconsistency resolves into one of the most systematic and learnable corners of Japanese grammar.

title: ている: habitual and occupational states
explanation: ている can also describe a habitual or ongoing occupational fact about someone — not a single action happening right now, but something generally true over an extended period, such as where someone works or what they regularly do.

examples.native: 銀行で働いています。
examples.gloss: I work at a bank.

examples.native: 毎朝走っています。
examples.gloss: I run every morning. (a regular habit)

bridge_note: English uses the simple present ("I work at a bank," not "I am working at a bank") for habitual facts, reserving "-ing" strictly for right-now actions. Japanese uses the same ている form for both the right-now progressive and the ongoing habitual/occupational sense, relying on context to distinguish them.
mistake: Translating 働いています literally as "am working" (implying only this very moment) when it's describing a standing occupational fact, not a momentary action.
branch: Aspect: ている and Related States

title: てある: resultative state of a transitive action (deliberate preparation)
explanation: てある attaches to a transitive verb and marks a resulting state that someone deliberately brought about, implying purpose — contrasted with the intransitive ている, which just states a resulting state with no implied agent or purpose.

examples.native: 窓が開けてある。
examples.gloss: The window has been opened (deliberately, for a reason).

examples.native: 窓が開いている。
examples.gloss: The window is open. (simple state, no implied agent or purpose)

bridge_note: English "the window is open" doesn't distinguish whether someone opened it on purpose for later benefit or it just happens to be open. Japanese's てある vs. ている pair encodes exactly that distinction: てある on a transitive verb signals deliberate preparation by an unstated agent, while ている on the intransitive counterpart is a neutral description of the current state.
mistake: Using ている where てある was meant (or vice versa) — the choice of verb (transitive 開ける vs. intransitive 開く) plus てある/ている is what carries the "on purpose" implication, not word choice alone.
source: Genki II grammar sequence (transitive/intransitive + てある); Tobira-level refinement
branch: Aspect: ている and Related States

title: ておく: doing something in advance / for later
explanation: て-form + おく marks an action deliberately done in advance, in preparation for something later. In casual speech it's often contracted to 〜とく.

examples.native: ホテルを予約しておきます。
examples.gloss: I'll book the hotel in advance.

examples.native: 飲み物を買っておくね。
examples.gloss: I'll go ahead and buy some drinks. (casual, and I'll leave them ready for later)

bridge_note: English expresses this idea with an added phrase like "in advance" or "ahead of time." Japanese folds that same forward-looking, preparatory nuance directly into the verb via おく (literally "to place/set down"), so the preparation-for-later meaning is grammaticalized rather than stated with extra words.
mistake: Confusing ておく (deliberate preparation for later) with plain ている (ongoing/resultative state) — they look similar but carry different implications about intent and timing.
branch: Aspect: ている and Related States

title: てしまう: completion, often with regret
explanation: て-form + しまう marks that an action was completed fully/irreversibly, and frequently carries a nuance of regret, surprise, or "oops" about an unintended outcome. In casual speech it's often contracted to 〜ちゃう.

examples.native: ケーキを全部食べてしまった。
examples.gloss: I ended up eating the whole cake. (with a nuance of "I shouldn't have")

examples.native: 宿題を忘れちゃった。
examples.gloss: I totally forgot my homework. (casual てしまう→ちゃう contraction)

bridge_note: English conveys the same "finished it completely, and maybe regrettably" idea with tone of voice or an added phrase ("I went ahead and ate the whole thing"). Japanese grammaticalizes that nuance directly into the verb with しまう, so the regret/completion coloring is built into the sentence itself rather than left to intonation.
mistake: Using てしまう for a neutral completed action with no regret nuance intended — it usually signals the speaker feels something was excessive, unintended, or a little unfortunate, not just "finished."
branch: Aspect: ている and Related States

title: たい — saying what you want to do
explanation: Attach たい to a verb's ます-stem to say the speaker wants to do that action. たい then conjugates exactly like an い-adjective, so it gets its own past and negative forms (たかった, たくない) independent of the verb it's built from.

examples.native: 日本に行きたいです。
examples.gloss: I want to go to Japan.

examples.native: もう食べたくないです。
examples.gloss: I don't want to eat any more.

bridge_note: English "want to" works the same way no matter whose desire it is. Japanese たい is grammatically locked to the speaker's own (or, in a question, the listener's) desire — describing someone else's want requires switching to an entirely different form.
mistake: Using たい for a third party (彼は行きたいです ✗) — for someone else's observed desire, use たがっている instead (彼は行きたがっている ✓).

title: ほしい — wanting a thing, and てほしい — wanting someone to do something
explanation: ほしい is an い-adjective meaning "wanted/desired," used with が to say the speaker wants an object. Attached to a verb's て-form, てほしい shifts to "I want you/someone to do [verb]."

examples.native: 新しい車がほしいです。
examples.gloss: I want a new car.

examples.native: もっとゆっくり話してほしいです。
examples.gloss: I want you to speak more slowly.

bridge_note: English uses the same verb "want" whether the object is a thing or another person's action ("I want a car" / "I want you to speak slowly"). Japanese uses one adjective, ほしい, for objects and pairs it with the て-form for actions, keeping both meanings under a single word instead of two separate verbs.
mistake: Marking the wanted item with を instead of が (車をほしいです ✗ → 車がほしいです ✓), since ほしい is an adjective describing the item, not a verb acting on it.

title: Potential form — saying what you can do
explanation: Every verb has a potential form meaning "can do [verb]." Ichidan verbs drop る and add られる (食べる→食べられる); godan verbs shift their final syllable to the e-row and add る (書く→書ける); the irregulars are する→できる and 来る→来られる. Because it becomes a stative verb, the thing you're capable of is usually marked with が rather than を.

examples.native: 日本語が話せます。
examples.gloss: I can speak Japanese.

examples.native: 漢字が読める人はまだ少ないです。
examples.gloss: There are still few people who can read kanji.

bridge_note: English adds a separate modal verb, "can," in front of the action verb.
