Japanese instead reshapes the verb itself into a new stative form, and that shift to a stative meaning is also why the object switches from を to が — the sentence is now describing a state ("Japanese is speak-able to me"), not an action performed on an object.
mistake: Keeping を on the potential object out of habit (日本語を話せます, widely tolerated in casual speech but the textbook-correct particle is が: 日本語が話せます). Also note the casual ら抜き (ra-nuki) shortcut, 食べれる for 食べられる — fine in conversation, avoid on exams.

title: Plain volitional form — "let's..." / "I shall..."
explanation: The plain volitional form (食べよう, 行こう) is the casual counterpart of the polite ましょう form. It's used to propose an action to someone close to you, or to voice your own resolve to do something.

examples.native: 一緒にお昼を食べよう。
examples.gloss: Let's eat lunch together.

examples.native: 今日は早く寝よう。
examples.gloss: I'll go to bed early today.

bridge_note: English "let's" and "I shall/will" are separate constructions. Japanese folds both meanings — proposing to someone and stating your own intention — into the same single conjugated verb form, distinguished only by context.

title: (よ)うと思う — "I'm thinking of doing..."
explanation: Attaching と思う ("I think that") to the volitional form expresses a present intention that's somewhat tentative — closer to "I'm thinking I'll..." than a firm plan.

examples.native: 来年、日本に行こうと思っています。
examples.gloss: I'm thinking of going to Japan next year.

bridge_note: English marks tentativeness with hedging words ("I'm thinking I might..."). Japanese builds the same tentativeness structurally, by wrapping the volitional form in a quoting "I think" clause rather than changing the main verb itself.
mistake: Using the plain volitional alone (行こう) when a reported intention is meant — 行こうと思う softens it into "I'm considering," while bare 行こう is closer to a direct "I will go / let's go."

title: つもり — a firmer "intend to / plan to"
explanation: つもり attaches to a verb's plain non-past form to state a settled intention or plan, sturdier than the more tentative (よ)うと思う.

examples.native: 来月、引っ越すつもりです。
examples.gloss: I plan to move next month.

examples.native: 彼女に本当のことを言うつもりはない。
examples.gloss: I have no intention of telling her the truth.

bridge_note: English distinguishes "I'm thinking of..." from "I plan to..." with different verb choices. Japanese draws the same line between (よ)うと思う and つもり, letting the grammatical pattern itself signal how firm the intention is.

title: の nominalizer — turning a verb clause into a noun (personal/perceived)
explanation: の attaches after a plain-form verb clause to turn the whole clause into a noun phrase, so it can be the subject or object of another verb. の is preferred when the clause describes something directly perceived or personally experienced, like watching or listening to something happen.

examples.native: 映画を見るのが好きです。
examples.gloss: I like watching movies.

examples.native: 子供が歌っているのを聞きました。
examples.gloss: I heard the child singing.

bridge_note: English uses the gerund ("-ing") to turn a verb into a noun-like object ("watching movies"). Japanese instead tacks a small nominalizing particle, の, onto the end of a full clause, letting an entire sentence — not just one verb — act as the noun.

title: こと nominalizer — turning a verb clause into a noun (facts/abstractions)
explanation: こと also nominalizes a plain-form verb clause, but it's used for facts, abstractions, and set grammatical patterns rather than something directly perceived — including the fixed expressions ことができる ("can do") and ことがある ("there is such a thing as / have done before"). の and こと overlap in many cases, but some contexts require specifically one or the other.

examples.native: 日本語を話すことができます。
examples.gloss: I am able to speak Japanese.

examples.native: 彼の趣味は絵を描くことです。
examples.gloss: His hobby is drawing pictures.

bridge_note: English again just uses "-ing" or "to" regardless of whether the nominalized idea is a live perception or an abstract fact. Japanese splits this into two competing nominalizers, の and こと, and picking the wrong one for a fixed pattern like ことができる is a genuine grammar error, not just an awkward phrasing.
mistake: Swapping の and こと freely — some set patterns only accept one (ことができる, ことがある never take の in these fixed forms), even though in freer contexts either can sound acceptable.

title: ことがある — "have done before" vs. "there are times when"
explanation: Attached to a verb's plain past form, ことがある reports a past experience ("I have done X before"). Attached to the plain non-past form instead, the same pattern shifts meaning to describe an occasional, recurring situation ("there are times when...").

examples.native: 日本に行ったことがあります。
examples.gloss: I have been to Japan before.

examples.native: たまに朝ごはんを食べないことがあります。
examples.gloss: There are occasionally times when I don't eat breakfast.

bridge_note: English marks life experience with a whole separate tense, the present perfect ("I have been to Japan"). Japanese instead reuses ordinary past/non-past verb forms and lets the fixed phrase ことがある do the work — and the same phrase means something entirely different depending on which tense feeds into it.
mistake: Using the non-past verb form when reporting a one-time past experience (日本に行くことがあります ✗ for "I've been to Japan") — experience specifically requires the past-tense verb before ことがある.

title: あげる — giving outward, away from the speaker
explanation: あげる means "give," but only when the direction of giving moves away from the speaker's own perspective — from the speaker (or someone in their in-group) to someone else. The giver is the subject; the receiver is marked with に.

examples.native: 私は友達に本をあげました。
examples.gloss: I gave my friend a book.

examples.native: 妹に花をあげました。
examples.gloss: I gave my little sister some flowers.

bridge_note: English "give" is direction-neutral — it works the same whichever way the gift moves. Japanese instead has a whole family of "give" verbs, and あげる is specifically the one for gifts leaving the speaker's own sphere; it can't be used for a gift arriving at the speaker.
mistake: Using あげる when the speaker is the one receiving (私に本をあげる ✗) — a gift coming toward the speaker always requires くれる instead.

title: くれる — giving inward, toward the speaker or their in-group
explanation: くれる also means "give," but for the opposite direction from あげる: something moving toward the speaker (or someone the speaker feels close to). The giver is the subject, marked with が; the receiver (the speaker or their in-group) is marked with に.

examples.native: 友達が私に本をくれました。
examples.gloss: My friend gave me a book.

examples.native: 先生が息子にお菓子をくれました。
examples.gloss: The teacher gave my son some candy.

bridge_note: English "give" doesn't care which way the gift travels relative to the speaker. Japanese bakes the speaker's own viewpoint and the uchi/soto (in-group/out-group) distinction directly into the choice of verb, something English grammar has no mechanism for at all.
mistake: Defaulting to あげる when the gift actually comes to the speaker (私に本をあげる ✗ → 私に本をくれる ✓) — this is one of the most common beginner errors in the whole giving/receiving system.
long_form:
English "give" is a completely direction-neutral verb: "I gave him a book" and "he gave me a book" use the identical verb, and the only thing that changes is which noun phrase sits in the subject slot. Japanese refuses to let a single verb cover both directions, and the reason is not merely lexical richness for its own sake — it's that the giving/receiving system is one of the places where Japanese grammar has fully absorbed a perspectival requirement: every act of giving must be narrated from somebody's specific point of view, and the verb itself has to name whose. あげる is reserved for gifts moving away from the speaker's own sphere (or the sphere of whoever the sentence's viewpoint is anchored to); くれる is reserved for the mirror-image direction, gifts arriving into the speaker's own sphere or that of someone the speaker feels close to (a family member, a friend, anyone the speaker is implicitly grouping with themselves — the same uchi "in-group" concept the curriculum returns to explicitly in the keigo unit). 友達が私に本をくれた and I 私は友達に本をあげた are not stylistic variants of the same event narrated two ways — they are two different verbs assigned by a grammatical rule that has nothing to do with formality and everything to do with which way the object crossed the uchi/soto boundary relative to the speaker.

This is worth situating historically and cross-linguistically, because it's easy to file "Japanese has three give-verbs" under quirky vocabulary trivia when it's really a manifestation of something bigger: Japanese grammar systematically encodes the speaker's own vantage point and social affiliation into verb choice far more pervasively than English does, and giving/receiving is simply the first place in the curriculum a learner meets this head-on (keigo, in Unit 10, and the adversative passive, in Unit 13, are the same underlying phenomenon — perspective and social distance baked into verb morphology — showing up again in different guises). Some linguists describe Japanese as having grammaticalized "empathy" or viewpoint into its verb system in a way most Indo-European languages simply haven't; English narrates events from something closer to an external, neutral camera position, and any perspectival flavor ("he was kind enough to give me a book" versus the flat "he gave me a book") has to be added lexically, as an optional editorial comment, rather than being a mandatory grammatical choice baked into the verb itself.

That grammatical mandatoriness is exactly why the classic beginner error — reaching for あげる when the gift is actually arriving toward the speaker — is so persistent and so revealing: it isn't a vocabulary slip, it's evidence that the learner is still narrating the event from an English-style neutral, direction-blind stance and hasn't yet internalized that Japanese requires picking a side before the sentence can even be built. 私に本をあげる is not just stylistically off, the way choosing a slightly wrong synonym would be — it's close to grammatically self-contradictory, since あげる specifically asserts an outward-from-speaker direction that the に私 phrase directly contradicts. The fix native speakers rely on, and that eventually becomes automatic for fluent learners, is to ask "whose side is this sentence being told from" before choosing the verb, not "what's a good word for give" — once giving/receiving verbs are treated as directional deictic markers (like English "come" versus "go," which do encode a similar toward-speaker/away-from-speaker split, just for motion rather than transfer) rather than as synonyms for a single neutral concept, the three-way system stops feeling arbitrary and starts feeling like the same logic English already applies to a smaller domain, just extended to cover transfer of objects as well as movement of people.

One more layer the short card doesn't have room for: this same viewpoint machinery extends past literal gift-giving into the benefactive constructions built on the te-form (てあげる/てくれる/てもらう, covered next), where the choice of helper verb signals not who transferred an object but who did a favor for whom — and native speakers lean toward てくれる specifically because it frames the other person's action as a kindness extended toward the speaker's side, carrying a warmth that てもらう's more clinical "I received [the favor of] your doing X" doesn't quite convey. Once you can hear that warmth difference, giving/receiving stops being a grammar unit about presents and starts looking like what it actually is: a fully worked-out system for expressing gratitude and social closeness through nothing but verb choice.

title: もらう — receiving, framed from the receiver's side
explanation: もらう means "receive." Unlike あげる/くれる, which are framed around the giver, もらう puts the receiver in the subject slot; the giver is marked with に or から.

examples.native: 私は友達に本をもらいました。
examples.gloss: I received a book from my friend.

examples.native: 先生から手紙をもらいました。
examples.gloss: I got a letter from my teacher.

bridge_note: English "receive from" already puts the receiver first, so もらう maps fairly directly onto English structure — but that similarity makes it easy to carelessly reverse who's the subject when translating the other two give-verbs, which don't map so directly.
mistake: Reversing subject and giver — 田中さんは私に本をもらいました means "Mr. Tanaka received a book from me," not the other way around; the receiver is always the grammatical subject of もらう.

title: てあげる / てくれる / てもらう — favors done as actions, not just gifts
explanation: Attaching あげる, くれる, or もらう to a verb's て-form extends the same giving/receiving logic from physical objects to actions done as favors, with the same directionality rules as the plain verbs.

examples.native: 友達が手伝ってくれました。
examples.gloss: My friend was kind enough to help me out.

examples.native: 先生に説明してもらいました。
examples.gloss: I had the teacher explain it to me.

bridge_note: English describes a favor with a plain declarative sentence and, separately, a "thank you" ("my friend helped me — thanks!"). Japanese folds the gratitude and the direction of the favor directly into the verb ending itself, so the warmth is grammatically obligatory, not optional.
mistake: Defaulting to てもらった when てくれた is more natural — 友達に手伝ってもらった ("I had my friend help me," more matter-of-fact) undersells the favor compared to 友達が手伝ってくれた ("my friend kindly helped me," which foregrounds the other person's kindness).

title: Honorific/humble giving verbs — a preview of keigo
explanation: The three giving/receiving verbs each have a formal counterpart used in keigo (respectful/humble speech): さしあげる is the humble version of あげる, くださる the honorific version of くれる, and いただく the humble version of もらう. Full use of these belongs to the keigo system covered next.

examples.native: 先生がおみやげをくださいました。
examples.gloss: My teacher was kind enough to give me a souvenir.

examples.native: 先生に本をいただきました。
examples.gloss: I received a book from my teacher (humbly).

bridge_note: English politeness is a matter of tone and word choice layered on top of the same verb "give." Japanese swaps in a completely different verb root for the formal register, the same pattern that recurs throughout the keigo system.

title: Teineigo — the baseline polite register
explanation: Teineigo is the polite です/ます register learners meet first, extended here with the polite prefixes お/ご on nouns (お茶, ご飯) and the more formal copula でございます. It's the neutral, safe register for talking to strangers or in public without being especially deferential or humble.

examples.native: お茶をどうぞ。
examples.gloss: Please, have some tea.

examples.native: こちらはロビーでございます。
examples.gloss: This is the lobby. (formal, e.g. a hotel employee speaking)

bridge_note: English politeness lives mostly in word choice and softening phrases ("could you possibly..."). Japanese teineigo is a distinct, obligatory grammatical layer — even the humble prefixes お/ご attach directly onto ordinary nouns, not just onto requests.

title: Sonkeigo (respectful) — the regular patterns
explanation: Sonkeigo elevates the person you're talking about (never the speaker) by dressing up their actions in extra-respectful grammar. The two productive patterns are お + ます-stem + になる (お読みになる, "to read," respectfully) and the れる/られる honorific, which reuses the same shape as the passive form (書かれる, "[he] writes," respectfully).

examples.native: 部長は明日、報告書をお読みになります。
examples.gloss: The department head will read the report tomorrow. (respectful)

examples.native: 先生はもう帰られました。
examples.gloss: The teacher has already gone home. (respectful)

bridge_note: English respect is expressed through titles and tone ("Would the director like to..."), never by re-conjugating the verb itself. Japanese sonkeigo grammatically transforms the verb whenever the subject is someone the speaker is elevating.
mistake: Using the れる/られる honorific and the plain potential/passive interchangeably without noting they share an identical conjugated shape — context (an elevated subject vs. an ability/passive meaning) is the only way to tell them apart.

title: Sonkeigo — irregular (suppletive) respectful verbs
explanation: A small set of very common verbs don't take the regular sonkeigo pattern — they switch to an entirely different, dedicated respectful verb: いらっしゃる covers いる/行く/来る, おっしゃる covers 言う, 召し上がる covers 食べる/飲む, なさる covers する, and ご覧になる covers 見る.

examples.native: 社長は今、会議室にいらっしゃいます。
examples.gloss: The president is in the meeting room right now. (respectful)

examples.native: 何を召し上がりますか。
examples.gloss: What will you have (to eat/drink)? (respectful)

bridge_note: English has a handful of similar swaps for extreme formality ("dine" instead of "eat"), but they're stylistic choices, not a required grammatical system. Japanese requires these specific suppletive verbs whenever sonkeigo applies to these particular actions — there's no regular-pattern fallback for them.
mistake: Applying the regular お+ます-stem+になる pattern to these verbs instead of using the suppletive form (お食べになる is heard but 召し上がる is the standard, more natural sonkeigo for 食べる).

title: Kenjougo (humble) — the regular pattern
explanation: Kenjougo lowers the speaker's own actions to indirectly elevate the listener. The productive pattern is お + ます-stem + する (or the more formal いたす): お持ちします, "I'll carry it (for you)," humbly.

examples.native: お荷物をお持ちします。
examples.gloss: Let me carry your luggage (for you).

examples.native: その件については後でご連絡いたします。
examples.gloss: I will contact you about that matter later. (humble)

bridge_note: English humility is conveyed through phrasing ("allow me to...", "if I may..."), never a grammatical downgrade of the verb itself. Japanese kenjougo is a fixed conjugation pattern applied specifically to the speaker's own actions, distinct from — and never used for — the listener's.
mistake: Mixing up sonkeigo and kenjougo direction — お持ちします describes something the speaker does, never something the listener does; using it for the listener's action would be backwards.

title: Kenjougo — irregular (suppletive) humble verbs
explanation: As with sonkeigo, a set of common verbs use a dedicated humble verb instead of the regular pattern: 参る covers 行く/来る, 申す/申し上げる covers 言う, いただく covers 食べる/飲む/もらう, 拝見する covers 見る, and おる covers いる.

examples.native: 明日、御社に参ります。
examples.gloss: I will come to your company tomorrow. (humble)

examples.native: 田中と申します。
examples.gloss: My name is Tanaka. (humble self-introduction)

bridge_note: English self-introductions stay grammatically identical regardless of formality ("I'm Tanaka" vs. "My name is Tanaka" is just a style choice). Japanese swaps in an entirely different humble verb, 申す, for exactly this kind of formal self-reference — the grammar itself, not just the vocabulary, marks the humility.

title: Choosing sonkeigo vs. kenjougo by uchi/soto (in-group vs. out-group)
explanation: Keigo isn't just "formal vs. casual" — the choice between elevating someone (sonkeigo) and lowering yourself (kenjougo) depends on the uchi/soto (in-group/out-group) relationship in the moment. The key twist: when speaking to an outsider (e.g. a client), you use humble forms even for your own boss's actions, because relative to that outsider, your boss now counts as part of your in-group.

examples.native: （客に）部長はただいま席を外しております。
examples.gloss: (To a client) Our department head is away from his desk at the moment. (humble form used for the boss, because the boss is "in-group" relative to the outside client)

bridge_note: English formality is fairly fixed regardless of audience — you'd describe your boss the same way to a client or a coworker. Japanese keigo grammaticalizes the social distance itself, so the exact same person's action gets a respectful verb in one context and a humble verb in another, depending only on who's listening.
mistake: Using sonkeigo (elevating) for your own in-group's actions when speaking to an outsider — describing your own boss with いらっしゃる to a client is backwards; it should be humble おる/参る, since the boss is "your side" from the client's point of view.
long_form:
It is tempting to file keigo under "Japanese formality" and treat it as a more elaborate version of the English formal-versus-casual register distinction — using "may I" instead of "can I," addressing someone as "Dr. Tanaka" instead of by first name. That framing captures teineigo (the baseline polite です/ます register) reasonably well, but it badly undersells sonkeigo and kenjougo, because those two registers aren't graded points on a single formality dial at all — they're a relational system that requires tracking, moment to moment, who is inside your in-group (uchi) and who is outside it (soto) relative to the specific person you're currently addressing. Sonkeigo elevates the actions of someone outside your immediate circle, or above you in status; kenjougo lowers your own actions (or your in-group's actions) to create the same relative elevation from the other direction. Crucially, these are not fixed labels permanently attached to specific people — they are computed fresh, in real time, based on who's in the conversation.

The twist the entry highlights — describing your own boss's actions with humble kenjougo when speaking to an outside client, even though you'd use respectful sonkeigo for that same boss when speaking to a coworker — is the single clearest illustration that keigo is tracking relative social distance, not fixed rank. From a coworker's perspective, your boss outranks you and sits partly outside your immediate peer circle, so sonkeigo (いらっしゃる, "the boss is out/away") is appropriate. From a client's perspective, though, the boundary that matters has shifted: you and your boss are now both "inside" the company, a single uchi unit facing an outsider, so the correct move is to lower the whole company's actions — including the boss's — with kenjougo (部長はただいま席を外しております), which has the effect of implicitly elevating the client by comparison. The boss's actual social rank never changed; what changed is which boundary is operative in this specific conversation. This is genuinely disorienting for English speakers precisely because English formality doesn't recompute itself based on who else is in the room the way keigo does — you'd describe your boss's whereabouts to a client in roughly the same words you'd use with a coworker, adjusting tone slightly but not swapping to a grammatically distinct verb system.

Historically, this system is one of the more thoroughly worked-out honorific grammars among the world's languages (Korean has a broadly comparable, independently evolved system; most European languages, by contrast, mark politeness mainly through pronoun choice — tu/vous, du/Sie — a far shallower mechanism by comparison). Japanese keigo grammaticalizes hierarchy and group-boundary awareness so deeply that it has its own dedicated, partly suppletive verb vocabulary (いらっしゃる, おっしゃる, 参る, 申す — verbs that exist for no purpose other than encoding respect or humility, with no register-neutral use at all), rather than layering politeness onto ordinary verbs through affixes alone the way the regular お+stem+になる/する patterns do. This suggests keigo isn't a late add-on to Japanese grammar but a deeply entrenched, historically old feature of the language reflecting a broader cultural emphasis on situational hierarchy and group identity — a genuine window into how a language can encode social structure directly into its verb morphology rather than leaving it to vocabulary choice and tone alone, the way English does.

The practical mistake this produces in learners is almost always directional confusion rather than simply forgetting a suppletive verb: using sonkeigo for your own in-group's actions when addressing an outsider (elevating your own boss in front of a client, which reads as either confused or subtly arrogant — as if you don't understand who the "insider" is in this exchange), or conversely staying casual in a setting that calls for the whole system to switch on. There's no shortcut around this beyond the one the sociolinguistics itself demands: before choosing sonkeigo or kenjougo, the real question is never "how formal is this occasion" but "relative to the person I'm speaking to right now, whose side is this action's actor standing on" — and that answer can flip mid-conversation the moment the audience changes, which is precisely what makes keigo the single most context-sensitive piece of grammar in the entire language.

title: と conditional — automatic, inevitable results
explanation: と links a condition to a result that follows naturally, automatically, or habitually every time — like a law of nature or a fixed routine. Because the result is treated as inevitable, と cannot be followed by a request, invitation, or expression of will in the main clause.

examples.native: 春になると桜が咲く。
examples.gloss: When spring comes, the cherry blossoms bloom.

examples.native: このボタンを押すと電気がつく。
examples.gloss: If you press this button, the light turns on.

bridge_note: English "when/if" doesn't care whether the result is a deliberate choice or an automatic consequence. Japanese と is grammatically restricted to automatic/habitual consequences, which is exactly why you can't use it to make a request or suggestion in the result clause.
mistake: Using と to make a request or suggestion (春になると花見に行こう ✗) — と's automatic-result meaning clashes with a volitional main clause; use たら or ば instead.

title: ば conditional — general hypotheticals and counterfactuals
explanation: ば forms a more formal/literary general hypothetical ("if X, then generally Y") and is also the form used in counterfactual regret expressions like 〜ばよかった ("if only I had..."). It resists a same-subject command or request in the main clause.

examples.native: 毎日練習すれば上手になります。
examples.gloss: If you practice every day, you'll get good at it.

examples.native: もっと早く出発すればよかった。
examples.gloss: I wish I had left earlier.

bridge_note: English "if only I had..." is its own fixed idiom, unrelated in form to an ordinary "if" clause. Japanese instead reuses the same ば conditional shape for both the general hypothetical and the counterfactual regret, just changing what follows it.
mistake: Using ば to directly command the same person who fulfills the condition (雨が降れば、家にいてください is a bit awkward) — ば prefers a general/impersonal result over a direct command aimed at the listener; たら handles that more naturally.

title: たら conditional — sequential "after/when," the safe default
explanation: たら presents a condition as something completed first, with the result following after. It's the most versatile of the four conditionals — it allows requests and volitional statements in the main clause, which makes it the safest default when unsure which conditional to use.

examples.native: 家に帰ったら、電話してください。
examples.gloss: When you get home, please call me.

examples.native: 宿題が終わったら、遊びに行こう。
examples.gloss: Once I finish my homework, let's go out and play.

bridge_note: English "when/after" already allows requests and suggestions freely ("when you get home, call me"), so たら maps onto English intuition more directly than と or ば do — which is exactly why it's the safest conditional to reach for as a learner.
source: Genki II Lesson 17 (たら/なら conditionals)

title: なら conditional — responding to something just said
explanation: なら presents a condition as a premise the speaker is reacting to — something the listener just mentioned or that's already on the table — rather than a new hypothetical. Uniquely among the four conditionals, なら's main clause can describe something that happens *before* the condition in real time.

examples.native: 日本に行くなら、京都がおすすめです。
examples.gloss: If you're going to Japan, I recommend Kyoto.

examples.native: 本を読むなら、電気をつけなさい。
examples.gloss: If you're going to read, turn the light on.

bridge_note: English "if" doesn't distinguish between a fresh hypothetical and a reaction to something already raised in conversation. Japanese なら is specifically reserved for the latter, and its ability to have the main-clause action happen chronologically first (turn the light on, then read) is a genuinely un-English piece of logic.
mistake: Using たら where なら is required — 本を読んだら電気をつけなさい ✗ wrongly implies turning the light on only after finishing reading; なら correctly frames "turn it on now, since you're about to read."
source: Genki II Lesson 17 (たら/なら conditionals)
long_form:
Japanese famously splits English's single word "if" across four distinct conditional forms (と, ば, たら, なら), and なら is the one that breaks the mold most dramatically, because it isn't really expressing a hypothetical about the world at all — it's expressing a hypothetical about the conversation. と, ば, and たら all describe some relationship between a condition and a result playing out in real or imagined time: spring arriving causes blossoms (と), practicing would lead to improvement (ば), getting home would be followed by a phone call (たら). なら instead takes as its "condition" something that has typically already been mentioned, implied, or is otherwise already live in the discourse, and responds to it: 日本に行くなら、京都がおすすめです isn't hypothesizing about whether the listener might go to Japan in some abstract sense — it's reacting to the fact that Japan-going is already on the table (the listener just said so, or the topic just came up), and offering advice conditioned on that already-established premise. This is why textbooks gloss なら as something closer to "if that's the case" or "given that" rather than a fresh, standalone "if."

That discourse-reactive nature produces なら's single strangest and most genuinely useful property: unlike the other three conditionals, なら's main clause can describe something that happens chronologically before the condition it's attached to. 本を読むなら、電気をつけなさい means "turn the light on now, since you're about to read" — the light-turning-on happens first, in preparation for the reading, even though なら-clauses are conventionally described as the "if" half of an if-then sentence. This would be flatly ungrammatical with たら, whose whole semantic core is sequential completion: the たら-clause's event has to finish before the main clause's event can follow it, which is exactly why 本を読んだら、電気をつけなさい is wrong for this meaning — it would absurdly instruct someone to turn the light on only after they've already finished reading in the dark. English has no direct equivalent to this logic because English "if" doesn't carry any inherent sequencing requirement one way or the other — "if you're going to read, turn the light on" sounds perfectly natural in English and doesn't strike an English speaker as needing special justification for its word order the way it would in Japanese, which is exactly why this is one of the harder N3-level distinctions for English speakers to internalize: there's no felt "problem" in English that なら is solving, so the whole distinction has to be learned as a genuinely new grammatical category rather than mapped onto an intuition English speakers already have.

Seeing all four conditionals side by side clarifies why Japanese needs this many words for what English handles with one: と is reserved for natural, mechanical, or habitual cause-and-effect with no room for a volitional main clause (you can't invite or command someone using と); ば leans hypothetical and slightly literary, comfortable with counterfactuals (「もっと勉強すればよかった」, "if only I'd studied more") but awkward with a same-subject command; たら is the safe, versatile, sequential default, equally at home with real past events, hypotheticals, requests, and invitations, which is exactly why textbooks teach it as the form to reach for when unsure; なら alone steps outside the time-ordered if-then logic the other three share, existing specifically to let a speaker respond to context rather than construct a new hypothetical from scratch. Framed this way, the four conditionals aren't four redundant ways to say the same thing needlessly split apart — they're four grammatically distinct tools solving four different communicative jobs that English happens to compress into one flexible word, relying on tone, context, and paraphrase to recover distinctions that Japanese requires the grammar itself to make explicit.

The common mistake — reaching for たら where なら is actually called for — is therefore not really a vocabulary slip but a logic error: it's mentally treating every "if you're planning to X" situation as sequential ("after X happens, then Y"), when the actual intended meaning is reactive-and-preparatory ("since X is already the plan, Y should happen now, in light of it"). Once a learner reframes なら not as "another word for if" but as "a way to respond conversationally to something already on the table, with no timing constraint on what follows," the form stops feeling like an arbitrary fourth conditional to memorize and starts feeling like exactly what it is: the one conditional built for advice-giving and reacting to what someone just said, which is why it shows up so heavily in exactly that kind of exchange in real conversation.

title: から vs. ので — subjective vs. objective reason
explanation: Both から and ので mean "because," but から frames the reason as the speaker's own subjective justification, while ので presents it as a softer, more objective-sounding cause-and-effect — which is why ので tends to sound more polite in formal or delicate situations.

examples.native: 忙しいから、行けません。
examples.gloss: I can't go, because I'm busy. (direct/personal justification)

examples.native: 忙しいので、行けません。
examples.gloss: I can't go, as I'm busy. (softer, more objective-sounding)

bridge_note: English "because" and "as/since" carry a similar subtle formality difference, but it's a stylistic nuance, not a required grammatical choice. Japanese speakers actively pick から or ので to manage how blunt or diplomatic a reason sounds, especially when declining or apologizing.

title: ため(に) — purpose vs. cause
explanation: ため(に) has two related but distinct uses: attached to a non-past verb or noun+の, it expresses purpose ("in order to"); attached to a past-tense verb or an adjective/noun, it expresses cause ("because of," often for an unwanted result).

examples.native: 日本語を勉強するために、日本に行きます。
examples.gloss: I'm going to Japan in order to study Japanese.

examples.native: 雨のため、試合は中止になりました。
examples.gloss: The game was cancelled because of the rain.

bridge_note: English uses two unrelated phrases, "in order to" and "because of," for these two meanings. Japanese uses the same ため(に) for both, distinguishing purpose from cause purely by what kind of word or tense comes right before it.
mistake: Using the non-past form when a past cause is meant (雨が降るため試合は中止になりました reads oddly for something that already happened) — the finished-cause reading calls for 雨のため or 雨が降ったため.

title: のに — "even though," with an edge of dissatisfaction
explanation: のに connects two clauses in an unexpected or disappointing contrast, similar to "even though," but it carries an emotional undertone of regret, surprise, or complaint that a neutral "even though" (ても) doesn't have.

examples.native: たくさん練習したのに、試合に勝てなかった。
examples.gloss: Even though I practiced a lot, I still couldn't win the match.

bridge_note: English "even though" is emotionally neutral by default; any frustration has to come from tone of voice or extra words ("...and that's so annoying"). Japanese builds that frustration directly into the grammar by choosing のに over the neutral ても.
mistake: Treating のに and ても as interchangeable — 練習したても勝てなかった would just be flatly reporting the contrast, while のに specifically signals the speaker feels let down or surprised by it.

title: せいで (blame) vs. おかげで (thanks to) — emotionally loaded cause
explanation: せいで and おかげで both mean roughly "because of," but they carry opposite emotional charge: せいで blames a negative outcome on its cause, while おかげで credits a positive outcome to its cause, often with a sense of gratitude.

examples.native: 寝坊したせいで、遅刻しました。
examples.gloss: Because I overslept, I was late. (blaming)

examples.native: 先生のおかげで、試験に合格しました。
examples.gloss: Thanks to my teacher, I passed the exam.

bridge_note: English "because of" is neutral, and blame or gratitude has to be added separately ("...which was totally my fault" / "...I'm so grateful"). Japanese splits "because of" into two dedicated words that carry the blame or gratitude built right into the grammar.
mistake: Using おかげで for a negative outcome, or せいで for a positive one — swapping them reverses the emotional tone entirely and can sound sarcastic if unintended.

title: Plain-form clauses modifying a noun — no relative pronoun needed
explanation: To describe a noun with a whole clause ("the book I bought yesterday"), Japanese simply places the entire clause, in its plain form, directly in front of the noun — no relative pronoun like "that" or "which," and no reordering of the clause itself.

examples.native: 昨日買った本はとても面白いです。
examples.gloss: The book I bought yesterday is very interesting.

examples.native: 私が住んでいる町は小さいです。
examples.gloss: The town I live in is small.

bridge_note: English needs "that/which" to glue a descriptive clause onto its noun, and the clause follows the noun. Japanese needs no connecting word at all, and the entire clause comes before the noun instead — a direct consequence of Japanese always putting modifiers ahead of what they modify.
mistake: Trying to insert a word for "that/which" or putting the clause after the noun, mirroring English order — Japanese pre-nominal clauses take neither; the clause simply sits immediately before the noun with nothing in between.
long_form:
English needs a relative pronoun — "that," "which," "who" — to attach a descriptive clause to a noun, and that pronoun does real syntactic work: it marks the boundary between the noun and the clause describing it, and it often signals what grammatical role the noun plays inside that clause ("who" for a subject, "whom" for an object, in careful English). Japanese does this job with nothing at all: no relative pronoun, no linking particle, not even a change in verb form. You simply take a complete plain-form clause — 昨日買った, "[I] bought [it] yesterday" — and place it directly in front of the noun it describes: 昨日買った本, "the book [I] bought yesterday." The clause is not missing anything; it is a fully grammatical plain-form sentence in its own right (the same plain past-tense た-form from Unit 5), just relocated to sit as a modifier ahead of a noun instead of standing alone as a complete utterance.

This zero-marking, no-pronoun-needed structure is a direct and completely predictable consequence of the head-final typology covered in Unit 2: if modifiers always precede the head they modify — adjectives before nouns, possessives before the thing possessed, particles after (not before) the nouns they govern — then a modifying clause is simply the largest, most elaborate modifier Japanese has, and it obeys the exact same placement rule as every smaller modifier. There's no special relative-clause machinery to learn here beyond that one placement principle; English, by contrast, needing a relative pronoun at all is really just a byproduct of English's own head-initial structure — the noun comes first, so English needs some overt signal to tell the listener "what follows next describes what you just heard," which is precisely the job "that/which" performs. Japanese doesn't need that signal because the modifying clause always comes first, so by the time the listener reaches the noun, they already know retroactively what it was that the preceding words were describing.

This creates the single most consistent parsing challenge intermediate learners face when moving from short sentences to real running text: English trains you to hear a noun and then wait to find out what modifies it; Japanese requires the opposite discipline — holding an entire clause in working memory, sometimes a long and internally complex one, without yet knowing which noun it's building toward, and only resolving the whole structure once the head noun finally arrives. 私が去年、京都で買った、とても高かった本 stacks reason, time, and place phrases (私が去年、京都で買った, "[that I] bought in Kyoto last year") plus an entire additional clause (とても高かった, "[that] was very expensive") all in front of a single noun (本, "book") — a construction that would need to be radically restructured into multiple relative clauses or a completely different sentence shape in English, because English relative clauses stacking after the noun get unwieldy and ambiguous very fast, while Japanese pre-nominal stacking, however cognitively demanding, remains grammatically unambiguous the whole way through since there's never any doubt about which noun the whole pile of clauses is building toward — it's always whatever comes immediately after the last one.

A nuance worth adding: unlike English relative clauses, Japanese pre-nominal clauses don't need any grammatical "gap" corresponding neatly to a relativized noun's role the way English requires ("the book that I bought___" — the gap is the object slot bought needs). Japanese modification is looser and more semantically driven — 昨日, 電話が鳴った時間 ("the time [when] the phone rang yesterday") modifies 時間 (time) even though 時間 isn't filling any argument slot inside 電話が鳴った at all; it's connected only by a plausible real-world relationship (the ringing happened at that time) rather than by a strict grammatical dependency. This is part of why "relative clause" is a slightly imprecise borrowed label for what Japanese is actually doing — a more accurate description is simply "any clause used adjectivally in front of a noun," a broader and more flexible category than the English relative clause it's usually equated with, and recognizing that flexibility helps explain constructions that would otherwise look like ungrammatical relative clauses if you're mentally translating the English rule too literally.

title: と quotation — direct and indirect speech
explanation: と marks a quoted clause before a verb like 言う ("say") or 思う ("think"), for both direct quotations (in 「」 brackets) and indirect/reported ones — Japanese doesn't grammatically distinguish direct from indirect speech the way English does with tense-shifting.

examples.native: 彼は「行く」と言いました。
examples.gloss: He said, "I'll go." (direct quote)

examples.native: 彼は行くと思います。
examples.gloss: I think he'll go. (indirect/reported thought)

bridge_note: English shifts verb tense when moving from direct to indirect quotation ("I'll go" → "he said he would go"). Japanese keeps the quoted clause's tense untouched either way and just marks it with と — the quoting particle does the work English does with tense-backshifting.

title: って — the casual stand-in for と and は
explanation: In casual speech, って can substitute for the quoting particle と (reporting what someone said or heard) or for the topic marker は, making sentences sound noticeably more conversational.

examples.native: 北海道って寒いって聞いた。
examples.gloss: I heard Hokkaido is cold.

bridge_note: English casual speech drops words and contracts phrases ("heard Hokkaido's cold") but doesn't swap in a distinct grammatical particle. Japanese って is a specific colloquial particle that does double duty for both quotation and topic-marking, which is why the same sentence can contain it twice with two different jobs.

title: という — naming and defining things
explanation: という attaches after a name, word, or quoted phrase to introduce or define it — "the thing/person called..." — and extends into set patterns like ということだ ("it means that...") and という意味 ("the meaning of...").

examples.native: 「桃太郎」という話を知っていますか。
examples.gloss: Do you know the story called "Momotaro"?

examples.native: 彼は来月引っ越すということです。
examples.gloss: I hear/it's said that he's moving next month.

bridge_note: English uses "called" or "named" as an ordinary adjective-like phrase ("the story called Momotaro"). Japanese treats という as a productive grammatical building block that also generates reported-speech and definitional patterns (ということだ, という意味), doing more grammatical work than the English equivalent.

title: か — embedding a question inside another sentence
explanation: か, the ordinary question-marking particle, can also embed a whole question clause inside a larger sentence, functioning like English "where/what/whether" clauses ("I don't know where to go").

examples.native: どこに行くか分かりません。
examples.gloss: I don't know where to go.

examples.native: 何を食べたいか教えてください。
examples.gloss: Please tell me what you'd like to eat.

bridge_note: English needs a specific set of question words repurposed as conjunctions ("where," "what," "whether") to embed a question. Japanese reuses the exact same か that ends a plain spoken question, just moving it inside the sentence instead of at the very end.

title: かどうか — "whether or not"
explanation: かどうか embeds a yes/no question into a larger sentence, equivalent to English "whether (or not)" — used when the embedded question has no question word (unlike plain embedded-か questions, which typically do).

examples.native: 明日、彼が来るかどうか分かりません。
examples.gloss: I don't know whether or not he'll come tomorrow.

bridge_note: English distinguishes "whether" (yes/no) from "where/what" (open question) with different words. Japanese marks the same distinction by adding どうか after か specifically for yes/no embedded questions, versus plain か alone for open questions with a question word.

title: Passive れる/られる — having something done to you
explanation: The passive form marks the grammatical subject as the receiver of an action rather than the doer. Ichidan verbs add られる (食べる→食べられる); godan verbs shift to the a-row and add れる (書く→書かれる); irregulars are する→される and 来る→来られる. The agent who performs the action is marked with に.

examples.native: 先生に褒められました。
examples.gloss: I was praised by the teacher.

examples.native: この本は多くの人に読まれています。
examples.gloss: This book is read by many people.

bridge_note: English marks the passive with "be + past participle" and an optional "by" phrase for the agent ("I was praised by the teacher"). Japanese conjugates the verb itself into a passive shape and marks the agent with に rather than a preposition equivalent to "by."
mistake: Confusing the passive with the potential form — for ichidan verbs they're identical in shape (食べられる can mean either "is eaten" or "can eat"), so only surrounding context disambiguates which one is meant.
long_form:
The Japanese passive looks, on the surface, like a direct translation of the English passive — both promote the receiver of an action into the grammatical subject slot, and both mark the original agent with a dedicated particle (English "by," Japanese に) rather than leaving it as a bare noun. 先生に褒められました and "I was praised by the teacher" line up almost word for word, and for a huge fraction of ordinary sentences that mapping holds up fine and Japanese passive can genuinely be learned as "the Japanese version of what English already does." Where the two systems pull apart is in how thoroughly optional the construction is: English passive is stylistic — you can always fall back to the active ("the teacher praised me") without losing any meaning beyond a shift in emphasis — while Japanese has an entire second class of passive sentence, the adversative or "suffering" passive, that has no active-voice equivalent to fall back to at all, because it's expressing something English simply doesn't have a grammatical slot for: that the subject was affected, inconvenienced, or put out by an event, even one they had no direct involvement in and even one built on a verb that isn't transitive in the first place. 雨に降られた ("I got rained on," in the sense of "the rain inconvenienced me") has no sensible active counterpart — "the rain rained me" isn't a sentence in either language — because 降る (to rain) doesn't take an object to promote into a passive subject. The passive morphology is doing something structurally different here: not demoting an agent and promoting a patient, but grafting an affected experiencer onto an event that would otherwise have no room for one.

This dual function — a genuinely transitive "regular" passive alongside an intransitive-friendly "adversative" passive built on the exact same morphology (れる/られる) — is one of the more linguistically striking features of Japanese grammar, and it's worth knowing that this isn't a coincidence of two unrelated grammatical accidents sharing a spelling. Historical linguists generally treat the adversative reading as an extension of the same underlying passive meaning — "having something happen to you" — stretched from its core transitive use (being the target of someone else's deliberate action) to cover the broader, looser sense of "being on the receiving end of an event's consequences," whether or not that event had a controllable agent or a direct object at all. Once you see the adversative passive as an extension of the same core meaning rather than an unrelated homophone, the two uses stop looking like two separate grammar points that happen to share a conjugation and start looking like one coherent concept — "this subject didn't cause the event, but the event happened to them" — applied across a wider range of verbs than English's passive voice was ever built to cover.

The ambiguity the short explanation flags — that ichidan verbs make passive and potential identical in shape (食べられる can mean either "is eaten" or "can eat") — is not a design flaw so much as a predictable side effect of how both forms were built historically: both the passive and the potential auxiliary trace back to related but distinct Old Japanese forms that ichidan conjugation patterns happened to converge on over time, while godan verbs, which conjugate through a wider set of vowel grades, kept the two forms distinct (書かれる passive versus 書ける potential). This is exactly the kind of detail a short flashcard has no room to explain but that removes the mystery once you see it: the ambiguity isn't scattered randomly across the whole verb system, it's confined specifically to the one verb class whose conjugation pattern doesn't have enough vowel-grade real estate to keep the two meanings apart, and context — almost always — supplies the missing disambiguation effortlessly for native speakers, the same way English speakers effortlessly disambiguate "I can't put my finger on it" from a literal finger-placing statement without noticing there was ever a choice to make.

Worth flagging as a genuine nuance for a more advanced learner: because Japanese passive can be built from intransitive verbs at all (via the adversative reading), it sits somewhat outside the strict "promote object, demote subject" definition of passive voice that most European-language grammar terminology was built to describe — which is one reason some linguists specifically avoid calling it a single, uniform "passive voice" and instead treat direct/transitive passive and adversative/intransitive passive as two related but formally distinguishable constructions sharing one morpheme. You don't need that terminological precision to use the form correctly, but it explains why some reference grammars organize this topic differently than Genki-style textbooks do, and why a Japanese passive sentence can sometimes feel like it's doing something subtly more than its English gloss lets on.

title: The adversative ("suffering") passive — being inconvenienced by an event
explanation: Japanese extends the passive form to intransitive verbs to mark that the subject was negatively affected or inconvenienced by an event, even one nobody directly did to them — a use English's passive voice has no equivalent for.

examples.native: 雨に降られました。
examples.gloss: I got rained on (and it was a real inconvenience).

examples.native: 夜中に子供に泣かれて、眠れませんでした。
examples.gloss: My child cried in the middle of the night [on me], and I couldn't sleep.

bridge_note: English has no passive form for "it rained" — you can only add a separate comment ("and it ruined my day"). Japanese instead passivizes the ordinarily-intransitive verb 降る itself, and that passive form alone signals the speaker was inconvenienced, with no extra words needed.

title: Causative せる/させる — making or letting someone do something
explanation: The causative form expresses making or letting someone do an action. Ichidan verbs add させる (食べる→食べさせる); godan verbs shift to the a-row and add せる (書く→書かせる); irregulars are する→させる and 来る→来させる. The causee particle depends mainly on the base verb's transitivity: an intransitive verb takes を for its causee (学生を走らせる, "make the students run"); a transitive verb already has its direct object marked with を, so the causee must take に instead (子供に野菜を食べさせる). Only with intransitive verbs does a second choice open up — swapping in に for を there shifts the reading from compulsion toward permission (子供を歩かせる "make the child walk" vs. 子供に遊ばせる "let the child play").

examples.native: 母は子供に野菜を食べさせました。
examples.gloss: The mother made/let her child eat vegetables. (transitive 食べる already takes を for 野菜, so the causee 子供 takes に)

examples.native: 先生は学生を走らせました。
examples.gloss: The teacher made the students run. (intransitive 走る, so the causee takes を)

bridge_note: English uses two separate verbs, "make" (compulsion) and "let" (permission), for a distinction Japanese collapses into a single causative conjugation — context, and for intransitive verbs the に/を choice, decides whether it reads as compulsion or permission.
mistake: Assuming the causee's particle is chosen purely by compulsion vs. permission — the primary factor is the base verb's transitivity (transitive verbs require に because を is already the object's slot); compulsion-vs-permission only comes into play as a secondary choice, and only for intransitive verbs. Also assuming せる/させる only ever means "force" — 子供に遊ばせる can just as easily mean "let the child play."

title: Causative-passive せられる/させられる — being made to do something (unwillingly)
explanation: Passivizing the causative form produces the causative-passive, meaning "was made to do [verb]" against one's will: 食べさせられる. For godan verbs, the full せられる often contracts in speech to される (書かせられる → 書かされる) — except for godan verbs whose dictionary form already ends in す (話す, 貸す): 話させられる does not contract to 話さされる, since that collision of さ+される would be awkward and ambiguous. The person forced is the subject (marked with は/が); the person doing the forcing is marked with に.

examples.native: 子供の頃、母にピアノを習わせられました。
examples.gloss: When I was a child, my mother made me learn the piano (and I didn't want to).

examples.native: 上司に残業させられました。
examples.gloss: My boss made me work overtime.

bridge_note: English says "was made to do X" without any built-in emotional coloring — reluctance has to be added separately ("...and I hated it"). Japanese stacks the adversative-passive nuance directly onto the causative, so the causative-passive form itself already signals the subject didn't want to do it.
mistake: Over-conjugating with an extra さ (書かせらせられる ✗ instead of the correct 書かせられる, contractible to 書かされる) and reversing the particles — the person forced is the subject, the forcer takes に, never the reverse. Also applying the される contraction to す-ending godan verbs (話さされる ✗) — those keep the full 話させられる.
long_form:
The causative-passive is often introduced as the "final boss" of Japanese verb conjugation, and there's a reason that reputation is earned rather than exaggerated: it's not a new form in its own right but a composition of two forms the learner already has, stacked on top of each other in sequence. Start with the plain verb 食べる, apply the causative (せる/させる, "make/let someone do"): 食べさせる, "make [someone] eat." Then apply the passive on top of that already-derived causative stem: 食べさせられる, "[the subject] was made to eat [by someone]." Nothing about the causative-passive's meaning is unpredictable once you treat it this way — it is simply "made-to-do," the passive of "made to do," built by the completely regular process of feeding one derived verb form as the input to the next derivation, which is exactly the "agglutinative principle" the curriculum names explicitly back in Unit 4: Japanese verbs are built by gluing meaningful suffixes onto a stem in a fixed pipeline order, and the causative-passive is simply the pipeline running two stages deep instead of one.

What makes the causative-passive feel disproportionately hard, despite being mechanically regular, is that its meaning inherits something extra from combining these two particular forms specifically: the causative alone is emotionally neutral (母にピアノを習わせた, "mother had me learn piano," carries no built-in judgment about whether the child wanted to), but stacking the passive on top pulls in exactly the adversative flavor the passive-form entry describes — being affected, put out, inconvenienced by an event. The causative-passive therefore doesn't just mean "was made to do X" in some flat, procedural sense; it inherently carries reluctance, the sense that the subject didn't want to do this and is reporting it with at least a trace of complaint. English "was made to learn piano" needs an explicit added clause ("...and I hated every minute of it") to convey that same reluctance, because English's passive-of-causative construction, if you can even build one naturally, doesn't inherit adversative coloring from anywhere — English simply has no grammatical mechanism analogous to the Japanese adversative passive for that coloring to come from in the first place. This is a genuinely elegant case of grammatical composition producing an emergent meaning greater than the simple sum of "causative" plus "passive" would predict on paper.

The contraction pattern for godan verbs — 書かせられる shortening in speech to 書かされる — is a real, productive colloquial sound simplification (せられ collapsing to され, a cluster reduction of exactly the kind that recurs throughout the history of Japanese verb morphology), and it's worth understanding why the entry singles out す-ending godan verbs (話す, 貸す) as immune to it: those verbs' causative-passive is 話させられる, and the contracted form would be 話さされる — but 話す's own dictionary stem already ends in さ, so the contraction would collide with, and become indistinguishable from, a different, unrelated sound sequence, creating exactly the kind of ambiguity the contraction exists to avoid in every other verb class. This is a small, specific phonological blocking condition, structurally the same kind of "don't apply this sound change if it would create confusion" logic that governs Lyman's Law blocking rendaku — the same general instinct in Japanese historical phonology (avoid changes that erase useful distinctions) showing up in two completely different corners of the grammar, centuries apart.

The most common learner error — adding an extra さ (書かせらせられる) — is best understood not as random sloppiness but as a kind of morphological over-application: having correctly identified that "causative" and "passive" are each marked by adding a syllable, a learner under cognitive load sometimes tries to mark them both again, once each, producing a doubled and ungrammatical result, roughly analogous to an English learner who, having correctly learned "-ed" marks the past tense, occasionally overgeneralizes and produces "goed." The other classic mistake — reversing who takes は/が and who takes に — is worth double-checking every time, because the logic here is genuinely counterintuitive relative to the plain causative: in 母にピアノを習わせられた, the speaker (the one forced) is the subject, and 母 (the forcer) takes に, which is the exact mirror image of what a learner's instinct might predict if they're thinking of causative-passive as "who's doing the causing" rather than "who's the affected party being reported on" — and remembering that the subject slot in any Japanese sentence, including this one, is reserved for whoever the sentence is fundamentally about, not necessarily whoever is grammatically most active, is the same lesson the topic/subject distinction (は versus が) was teaching all the way back in Unit 2, now paying off three units later in the single most complex verb form in the whole curriculum.

title: そうだ — "looks like" vs. "I hear that"
explanation: そうだ has two unrelated attachments and meanings. The hearsay use attaches to the full plain form of a verb/adjective/noun+だ and reports something you heard: 雨が降るそうだ. The appearance/様態 use attaches to a verb ます-stem or adjective stem (dropping い, or だ for na-adjectives/nouns) and reports a visual impression: 雨が降りそうだ. Two irregulars for the appearance use: いい→よさそう, ない→なさそう.

examples.native: 天気予報によると、明日は雨が降るそうだ。
examples.gloss: According to the weather forecast, I hear it's going to rain tomorrow.

examples.native: この料理、美味しそうですね。
examples.gloss: This dish looks delicious, doesn't it?

bridge_note: English collapses both of these into a single vague "seems like"/"I heard," but Japanese grammaticalizes the distinction between secondhand report and direct sensory impression as two different conjugation patterns on the same word.
mistake: mixing up the two attachment patterns — hearsay uses the full plain form (寒いそうだ, not 寒そうだ for "I hear it's cold"), while appearance uses the stem (寒そうだ for "looks cold"). Also forgetting the よさそう/なさそう irregulars.

title: ようだ — subjective inference and comparison
explanation: ようだ expresses a conclusion the speaker draws from their own direct observation or sensory evidence, or draws a comparison ("like/as if"). It attaches to the plain form of a verb/i-adjective, な for na-adjectives, and の for nouns.

examples.native: 誰か来たようだ。
examples.gloss: It seems someone came [based on what I can see/hear].

examples.native: 彼はまるで子供のようだ。
examples.gloss: He's just like a child.

bridge_note: English "seems"/"as if" doesn't require choosing a different connective form depending on the word class it attaches to, the way ようだ's な/の attachment rules do.
mistake: confusing ようだ (inference from the speaker's own direct impression) with らしい (inference leaning on outside information/hearsay) — see the らしい entry for the contrast.
source: Genki II / Bunpro N3 pattern list

title: らしい — hearsay-flavored inference, or "typical of"
explanation: らしい marks an inference based on secondhand information or general impression, committing less than ようだ. It attaches directly to the plain form (na-adjectives and nouns drop だ). As a noun suffix, らしい also means "typical/characteristic of": 男らしい ("manly").

examples.native: 田中さんは来ないらしい。
examples.gloss: I hear/it seems Tanaka isn't coming.

examples.native: 彼らしい行動だ。
examples.gloss: That's such a typically-him thing to do.

bridge_note: English has no equivalent suffix that turns any noun into "typical of X" the way らしい does — it usually needs a whole phrase like "so like him."
mistake: part of the doc-flagged confusable trio そうだ／ようだ／らしい: らしい leans on outside information with a weaker personal commitment than ようだ (direct impression) or そうだ-hearsay (a specific quoted source).

title: みたい — casual "seems like / is like"
explanation: みたい is the colloquial counterpart of ようだ, expressing resemblance or inference. Unlike ようだ, it attaches directly after the plain form, noun, or na-adjective with no の/な needed.

examples.native: 雨みたい。
examples.gloss: Looks like rain.

examples.native: 彼はまるで先生みたいだ。
examples.gloss: He's just like a teacher.

bridge_note: Functions like casual spoken English "it's like..." — both are the informal register's stand-in for a more formal comparison word.
mistake: using みたい in formal writing or polite business speech, where ようだ is expected instead — みたい is inherently casual register.

title: かもしれない — "might / maybe"
explanation: かもしれない expresses low-commitment possibility. It attaches to the plain form (na-adjectives/nouns drop だ).

examples.native: 明日雨が降るかもしれない。
examples.gloss: It might rain tomorrow.

bridge_note: Maps closely onto English "might/may," but functions as a fixed grammatical suffix rather than a separate modal verb.
mistake: treating かもしれない as interchangeable with にちがいない or はず — it's the weakest-commitment of the three; using it for something you're actually sure of undersells your confidence.

title: にちがいない — "must be" (strong conviction)
explanation: にちがいない expresses strong conjecture — the speaker's own confident conclusion based on reasoning or evidence. It attaches to the plain form.

examples.native: 彼は忙しいにちがいない。
examples.gloss: He must be busy.

bridge_note: Parallels the epistemic English "must be," both grammaticalizing a strong subjective inference rather than a fact.
mistake: confusing with はず — にちがいない is the speaker's own strong personal conviction, while はず is grounded in objective reasoning or known facts (a schedule, a rule) rather than gut certainty.

title: はず — "should be / is supposed to be" (expectation)
explanation: はず expresses an expectation grounded in objective reasoning or known facts, not just a hunch. It attaches to the plain form (na-adjectives take な, nouns take の) + はず(だ). The negative はずがない means "there's no way that ~."

examples.native: 彼は今日来るはずだ。
examples.gloss: He's supposed to come today [I know his schedule].

bridge_note: Similar to the epistemic English "should" ("he should be here by now"), not the obligation sense of "should."
mistake: confusing with にちがいない — はず requires an objective basis (a schedule, a known fact), while にちがいない is a subjective, evidence-based hunch even without hard facts.
source: Genki II / Bunpro N3 pattern list

title: ようになる — "came to be able to / reached the point of"
explanation: ようになる marks a change of state or ability that develops over time, often not fully under the subject's control. It attaches to a verb's plain (frequently potential) form + ようになる.

examples.native: 漢字が読めるようになった。
examples.gloss: I've become able to read kanji.

bridge_note: English needs a whole phrase ("came to be able to") where Japanese has a single compact grammaticalized pattern for this change-of-state meaning.
mistake: confusing with ようにする — になる describes a change/result that occurs (not necessarily deliberately), while にする describes the subject's deliberate ongoing effort to bring something about.
source: Tobira intermediate grammar — placement straddles N3/N4 depending on source (contested — needs native/teacher review)

title: ようにする — "make an effort to / try to make it so that"
explanation: ようにする marks a deliberate, ongoing effort by the subject to bring about a state. It attaches to a verb's plain (dictionary or negative) form + ようにする, often as ようにしている for a standing habit/effort.

examples.native: 毎日運動するようにしている。
examples.gloss: I make an effort to exercise every day.

bridge_note: Closest to English "I try to make sure I ~," emphasizing ongoing deliberate effort rather than a single completed change.
mistake: confusing with ようになる — にする is the subject's deliberate effort, while になる is the (possibly unintentional) resulting change of state.

title: ことにする — "decide to" (speaker's own decision)
explanation: ことにする marks the subject's own deliberate decision. It attaches to a verb's plain form + ことにする.

examples.native: 来年留学することにした。
examples.gloss: I decided to study abroad next year.

bridge_note: Maps onto English "I decided to ~," while ことになる (its passive counterpart) maps onto "it's been decided that ~ / it turns out that ~."
mistake: confusing with ことになる — にする is the speaker's own active decision, while になる is a decision made by circumstances or someone else, presented as simply happening to the speaker.

title: ことになる — "it's been decided that / it turns out that"
explanation: ことになる presents a decision or outcome as arising from circumstances or someone else's choice, not the speaker's own volition. It attaches to a verb's plain form + ことになる.

examples.native: 来月大阪に転勤することになった。
examples.gloss: It's been decided that I'll be transferred to Osaka next month.

bridge_note: English marks this with a passive construction ("it has been decided"), while Japanese uses a dedicated grammatical pattern that also covers a softer "it turns out that" sense.
mistake: confused with ことにする (speaker's own active decision) and with the ようになる/ようにする pair — this is a doc-flagged contested placement (straddles N3/N4 depending on source; Tobira treats it as intermediate) — needs native/teacher review.
source: Tobira intermediate grammar — contested N3/N4 placement (contested — needs native/teacher review)

title: てくる — directional/temporal "come to do / start to"
explanation: てくる attaches to the te-form and marks movement toward the speaker or toward the present moment — either literal ("do X and come back") or a gradual change approaching now ("started to / has been ~ing up to now").

examples.native: 雨が降ってきた。
examples.gloss: It started to rain [and is still going].

examples.native: 単語を覚えてきた。
examples.gloss: I've been memorizing vocabulary [building up to now].

bridge_note: English lacks a grammaticalized "toward-the-present" aspect marker; it's usually rendered loosely with "started to" or "has been ~ing."
mistake: confusing directionality with ていく — てくる moves toward the speaker/present, ていく moves away/into the future.

title: ていく — directional/temporal "go on doing / do and go away"
explanation: ていく attaches to the te-form and marks movement away from the speaker, or a continuing trend heading into the future.

examples.native: これからも日本語を勉強していく。
examples.gloss: I'll keep studying Japanese from now on.

bridge_note: No single English auxiliary captures this "continuing away from now" sense; English typically just says "will keep ~ing."
mistake: confusing directionality with てくる — see that entry for the contrast.

title: ように — "so that" (non-volitional purpose)
explanation: ように expresses a purpose or goal involving a state the speaker can't directly will into being — typically a potential-form verb or an inherently non-volitional verb (わかる, 見える, 治る). It attaches to the verb's plain form.

examples.native: 忘れないようにメモしておいた。
examples.gloss: I wrote it down so that I wouldn't forget.

bridge_note: English "so that" doesn't distinguish volitional from non-volitional purpose clauses the way Japanese's ように/ために split does — this placement itself straddles N3/N4 by source (contested — needs native/teacher review).
mistake: confusing with ために: ように pairs with non-volitional predicates (potential form, involuntary verbs), while ために requires a same-subject volitional verb expressing a deliberate goal.
source: Bunpro N3 confusable-pairs module — placement contested across sources

title: ために — "in order to" (volitional purpose)
explanation: ために expresses a deliberate, volitional purpose pursued by the same subject as the main clause. It attaches to a verb's dictionary form, or noun + の. A separate, related use means "because of / for the sake of."

examples.native: 日本語を勉強するために日本に来た。
examples.gloss: I came to Japan in order to study Japanese.

bridge_note: Matches English "in order to," but Japanese reserves it strictly for volitional purpose, handing non-volitional purpose off to a separate word (ように).
mistake: confusing with ように — see that entry: ために needs a volitional verb and a deliberate goal, ように is used with potential/involuntary predicates.

title: ながら — "while" (simultaneous actions)
explanation: ながら attaches to a verb's ます-stem and joins two actions performed simultaneously by the same subject; the main action is the second, ながら-clause verb's subordinate.

examples.native: 音楽を聞きながら勉強する。
examples.gloss: I study while listening to music.

bridge_note: Directly parallels English "while ~ing," but Japanese fixes the word order (ながら-clause first, main clause second).
mistake: confusing with concessive ながら(も) ("although") — identical form, disambiguated only by whether the two clauses are simultaneous actions or a contradiction (see the N2 concessive entry).

title: たり…たり — representative actions from a set
explanation: たり…たりする lists a couple of representative actions out of a larger, implied set, rather than an exhaustive list. It attaches to the verb's plain past (た) form + り, usually given twice, ending in する (conjugated for tense).

examples.native: 週末は本を読んだり映画を見たりする。
examples.gloss: On weekends I do things like read books and watch movies [among other things].

bridge_note: Parallels English "do things like X and Y," explicitly signaling the list is illustrative, not complete — English usually needs to add "and so on" to convey the same thing.
mistake: listing every single action instead of just a couple of representative ones, or forgetting the closing する that the whole construction needs.

title: ばかり — "only / nothing but" (often critical)
explanation: ばかり limits to one thing, often with a nuance of excess or mild criticism. It attaches to a noun, or to a verb's た-form ("just did ~"), or te-form + いる ("does nothing but ~").

examples.native: 彼はゲームばかりしている。
examples.gloss: He does nothing but play games [and it's a bit much].

bridge_note: English "nothing but" can carry the same mild disapproval, but Japanese marks it with a dedicated particle rather than relying on tone alone.
mistake: confusing with だけ — だけ is a neutral "only," while ばかり typically implies the speaker thinks it's too much or one-sided.

title: だけ — "only" (neutral limiter)
explanation: だけ is a neutral limiter meaning "only/just," with no built-in judgment about whether that's too much or too little. It attaches directly to a noun, verb, or adjective in the plain form.

examples.native: 一つだけ買った。
examples.gloss: I bought only one.

bridge_note: Maps closely onto neutral English "only/just," unlike its more judgment-laden cousin ばかり.
mistake: confusing with ばかり (which implies excess/criticism) and with しか…ない (which requires a negative verb and emphasizes scarcity more strongly).

title: しか…ない — "nothing but" (obligatory negative)
explanation: しか…ない emphasizes scarcity more strongly than だけ, and requires a negative verb at the end of the sentence.

examples.native: お金が少ししかない。
examples.gloss: I only have a little money.

bridge_note: Closest to English "nothing but/only" used with an implicit negative slant ("I've got nothing but a little money").
mistake: forgetting the obligatory negative verb (しかある is ungrammatical); confusing with だけ, which needs no negative and carries a more neutral tone.

title: ほど — "to the extent of / as much as"
explanation: ほど expresses degree, often in a negative comparison (AはBほど〜ない, "A isn't as ~ as B"), or as a standalone degree marker ("to the extent that ~").

examples.native: 今日は昨日ほど寒くない。
examples.gloss: Today isn't as cold as yesterday.

examples.native: 死ぬほど疲れた。
examples.gloss: I'm tired to death [extremely tired].

bridge_note: Parallels English "as ~ as," but Japanese fixes the comparison inside a negative frame (AはBほど〜ない) rather than a direct "as...as" structure.
mistake: reversing the word order of the negative comparison — it must be AはBほど〜ない, not the other way around.

title: など — "and so on / things like" (neutral listing)
explanation: など gives non-exhaustive examples after a noun or list of nouns, roughly "such as ~, etc.," with no particular emotional coloring.

examples.native: りんごやみかんなどを買った。
examples.gloss: I bought things like apples, oranges, and so on.

bridge_note: Directly parallels neutral English "etc./and so on," unlike its emotionally-loaded cousin なんて.
mistake: confusing with なんて — など is neutral, while なんて adds a dismissive or surprised emotional tone that など never carries.

title: なんて — "the likes of / things like" (dismissive/surprised)
explanation: なんて marks a noun or quoted clause with a strong emotional coloring — surprise, disbelief, contempt, or self-deprecation.

examples.native: 私に彼女ができるなんて信じられない。
examples.gloss: I can't believe I'd get a girlfriend, of all things.

bridge_note: Similar to English "the likes of ~" or an incredulous "~, of all things," carrying built-in attitude rather than neutral listing.
mistake: confusing with neutral など — なんて always carries emotional coloring and would sound oddly dramatic in a plain, neutral list.

title: し — listing parallel reasons
explanation: し attaches to the plain form and connects clauses to list parallel facts or reasons that cumulatively support a conclusion, roughly "what's more, ~ and ~."

examples.native: この店は安いし、美味しいし、いつも行く。
examples.gloss: This place is cheap, and it's delicious, so I always go there.

bridge_note: Closest to English "what's more" stacking up reasons, rather than a simple noun-level "and" like と or や.
mistake: using し like a simple noun-connecting "and" (と/や) instead of its actual role: stacking up clause-level reasons toward a conclusion.

title: ものの — a calm, objective "although"
explanation: ものの attaches to the plain form and presents a fact followed by a contrasting, often disappointing, reality — a calm, objective concessive with no strong emotional charge.

examples.native: 日本語を三年間勉強したものの、まだうまく話せない。
examples.gloss: Although I've studied Japanese for three years, I still can't speak it well.

bridge_note: Matches formal English "although," landing more neutral/objective in tone than emotionally-charged concessives.
mistake: confusing with つつ(も) — つつ is more literary and restricted to verb ます-stems only, while ものの attaches broadly across word classes and reads naturally in both speech and writing.
source: well-corroborated N2 across sources (Bunpro, JLPT Sensei, Japanesetest4you)

title: つつ(も) — literary "while / even though"
explanation: つつ(も) attaches ONLY to a verb's ます-stem and expresses either simultaneous action or, more often in this use, a literary concessive: doing/knowing one thing while nonetheless doing another.

examples.native: 体に悪いと知りつつも、タバコをやめられない。
examples.gloss: Even though I know it's bad for my health, I can't quit smoking.

bridge_note: Closest to literary English "while knowing that ~, nonetheless..." — Japanese marks the register (written/formal) directly through the grammar choice.
mistake: confusing with ものの — つつ is restricted to ます-stem attachment and formal/written register, while ものの attaches more broadly and reads naturally in speech too.
source: well-corroborated N2 across sources (Bunpro, JLPT Sensei, Japanesetest4you)

title: ながら(も) — concessive "although / even though"
explanation: The concessive use of ながら(も) is distinct from the simultaneous-action ながら: it attaches to a verb's ます-stem, an i-adjective, or a na-adjective, and expresses a contradiction rather than two things happening at once.

examples.native: 悪いと知りながらも、つい嘘をついてしまった。
examples.gloss: Even though I knew it was wrong, I ended up lying.

bridge_note: English "even though" doesn't share a form with "while," but Japanese overloads ながら for both — context alone disambiguates.
mistake: confusing with the simultaneous-action ながら (see that entry) — identical form; tell them apart by whether the two clauses describe two things happening together or a contradiction.

title: にもかかわらず — formal "despite / in spite of"
explanation: にもかかわらず is a more formal, stronger concessive than のに. It attaches to the plain form, or directly after a noun (である)にもかかわらず.

examples.native: 大雨にもかかわらず、試合は行われた。
examples.gloss: Despite the heavy rain, the match was held.

bridge_note: Matches formal English "despite/in spite of," and like its English counterpart signals a written/formal register rather than casual speech.
mistake: using にもかかわらず in casual conversation where のに would sound more natural — it's a formal/written-register concessive, and learners often miss the register mismatch.
source: well-corroborated N2 across sources (Bunpro, JLPT Sensei, Japanesetest4you)

title: からこそ — emphatic "precisely because"
